lawyer:

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15th June, 2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3028 of 2003.)
full_judgment:
Md. Hassan Ameen J.: This petition for leave to appeal has been filed by the defendant-petitioner against the judgment and order dated 15th June,2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3028 of 2003 making the Rule absolute reversing the judgment and decree dated 29-03-2003 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Manikgonj in Title Appeal No.114 of 2001 allowing the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 24-05-2001 passed by a Senior Assistant Judge, Saturia, Manikgonj in Title Suit No.91 of 1999 dismissing the same.

<u>2. The case of the petitioner (opposite-party-plaintiff) before the trial Court was that he (plaintiff) instituted Title Suit No.91 of 1999 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Saturia, Manikgonj praying for a preliminary decree for partition of .10 decimals of land out of R. S. Plot Nos. 172 and 178 of Mouza Dasra under Police Station and District Manikgonj, stating in nutshell that the land under partition belonged to Amit Kumar Roy, who being in right, title and possession transferred 10 decimals of land by kabala No.966 dated 12-02-1996 in favour of the plaintiff and also transferred 15 decimals of land by another kabala being No.965 dated 12-02-1996 in favour of the defendant No. 1. There is a homestead on the land under partition. The plaintiff and the defendant jointly purchased the said homestead. The plaintiff and defendant used to possess the said homestead jointly through bharatia. The defendants have been abstaining from paying rent of the homestead in favour of the plaintiff since June, 1999. The plaintiff demanded partition on May, 1999 and the same was refused by the defendant and as such the suit was filed.</u>

<u>3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement, alleging, inter-alia, that the suit land measures an area of .30 decimals out of which .3 decimals of land fell into the road. Thereafter Amit Kumar Roy gave a proclamation for transfer of .30 decimals of land and also gave a proclamation separately for transfer for 'pucca' homestead standing upon the suit land. The price of the homestead was settled at Tk. 1,00,000/- the defendant purchased 15 decimals of land along with homestead and the plaintiff purchased only 10 decimals of land. The plaintiff as well as the defendant got possession in their purchased land. The defendant made a boundary wall covering his land, mutated his name and paid rent. The plaintiff did not purchase the homestead. The defendant possessed the same. The fact of payment of rent to the plaintiff is not true and accordingly, the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit.</u>

4. The trial Court in consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit by 1 the judgment and decree dated 24th May, 2001 against which the plaintiff-preferred Title appeal, No. 114 of 2001 which was allowed directing the plaintiff to file a separate suit in respect of the homestead property and further directed Advocate Commissioner, if appointed for allotment of necessary land providing an access of the plaintiff with the existing road. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied by the said judgment and decree, the defendant moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule. The High Court Division thereafter in consideration of evidence on record as well as facts and circumstances of the case discharged the Rule. Hence this leave petition.

5. Mr. Syed Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the petitioner-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 purchased the suit property in question by two separate registered deeds. He further submits that the High Court Division failed to show that the defendant-petitioner after purchase of .15 decimals of land from the same vendor mutated his name and paid rent to the Government and got water, gas and electricity connection as well as constructed boundary wall which was not objected by the plaintiff and as such the direction of the High Court Division for giving passage is beyond pleading and as such committed illegality in the decision and it merits consideration to dispose of the matter. Learned Advocate lastly submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the pleadings of the parties in their true perspective and traveled beyond the pleadings and thereby committed illegality and as such required to be interfered with.

6. We have heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner and perused the petition so filed and reasons to believe that there is no substance in the matter and as such no interference is called for in the findings and decisions of the High Court Division and accordingly it is dismissed.

End.

S.M. Munir, Advocate, instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellant.

case_source: (From Judgment and order dated 26.4.1995 Passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 914 of 1987)
full_judgment:
Md. Fazlul Haque, J.: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff arises out of the judgment and order dated 26.4.1995 passed by the Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 914 of 1987 making the Rule absolute and reversing the judgment and decree dated 8.7.1987 of the learned Additional District judge, Bagerhat passed in Title Appeal No. 181 of 1984 decreeing the suit and reversing the judgment and decree dated 7.2.1983 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Bagerhat in Title Suit No. 396 of 1975 dismissing the Suit.

2. Rakhal Chandra Pal as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 396 of 1975 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Bagerhat against the respondent No. 1 for declaration of title to the suit land along with huts thereon and for khas possession thereof.

3. The Case of the plaintiff, in short, is that 30 decimals of land of S.A. Khatian No. 16 corresponding to C.S. Khatian No. 116 of Mouza Bashabati belonged to Gobinda Bairagi under landlord Ambika Charan, Gobinda Bairagi died about 30-40 years back, (Gobinda Baragi died unmarried leaving no heir), landlord Ambika Charan made the suit land khas and took it under his own possession. After the death of Ambika Charan his son Manindra Nath, in the year of 1359 B. S. Settled the suit land orally to the plaintiff Rakhal Chandra Pal. Manindra Nath filed Rent suit No. 150 of 1956 wherein he admitted the present plaintiff as his tenant. On payment of arrear rents the suit was dismissed. The plaintiff had been in possession of the suit land having the Golpata hut oil it on 19.4.73 the defendant No. 1 dispossessed the plaintiff, hence the suit was filed.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement and contended, inter-alia that Gobinda Bairagi had although in passion of the suit land. He was married and dies leaving only one son and heir Bishweshwar Bairagi, who sold the said land to the defendant No. 1 by kabala dated 10.8.1972 and delivered possession of the suit land to him. The defendant No. 1 is in possession of the suit land by constructing hats on approved plan from Municipality. Plaintiff's allegation of making the suit land khas by Ambika Charan, the superior owner and settling the land orally by Monindra, Son of Ambika to the plaintiff is absolutely false and the plaintiff never possessed the suit land. The defendant No.1 further contended that the allegation of dispossession by him is also false.

5. The trial Court dismissed the suit disbelieving the case of the plaintiff that he had taken oral settlement of the land from Monindra Charan after making the suit land khas by superior landlord and delivered possession the plaintiff and dispossession from the suit land by the defendant No. 1. the trial court has believed that Gobinda Bairagi left his son, Bishashwar as his heir and that Bishashwar legally transferred the suit land to the defendant No. 1. Further, the trial court has held that tenancy of Gobinda Bairagi was not terminated legally and as such alleged settlement of suit land orally to the plaintiff is illegal. It appears that the appellate court believed the possession of the plaintiff, who was allegedly dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 Further appellate court has held that the appellate court believed the possession of the plaintiff, who was allegedly dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 Further appellate court has held that Gobinda Bairagi abandoned his rayoti right and then the landlord Ambika legally made the suit land khas, and his son Monindra settled the suit land orally to the plaintiff after the death of Ambika. The appellate court has relied on two documents, namely, a certificate from the local Chairman marked Ext. X and the voter list of the locality, which were filed for the first time before the appellate court and found that Gobinda Bairagi was unmarried and Bisheshwar was not his son. The High Court Division with regard to the aforesaid two documents has held that these two documents were not legally considered by the appellate Court as the same were not proved in accordance with law, and the same were not admitted as additional evidence in compliance with the provision of order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil procedure, yet the appellate court on the basis of those two documents has held that Gobinda Bairagi was unmarried and Bishashwar was not t his son. The High Court Division has held that the finding on the basis of that evidence is wrong because the said documents were not legally proved. Further, the High Court Division has held that the superior landlord could make the land of a rayoit khash and could take it under his own possession only in compliance of the provision of section 87(1) (2) of the Bengal Tenancy Act but the same was not done in the present case. Sub-sections 1 and 2 of Section 87 of B.T. Act are as under:-

"87(1) if a raiyat or under raiyat voluntarily abandons his residence without notice to his landlord and without arranging for payment his rent as it falls due and cases to cultivate his holding either by himself or by some other person, the landlord may, at any time after the expiration of the agricultural year in which the raiyat or under raiyat to abandons and ceases to cultivate, enter on the holding and let it to another tenant or take it into cultivation himself. (2) Before a landlord enters under this section, he shall file a notice in the prescribed form in the collectors office, stating that he has treated the holding as abandoned and is about to enter on it accordingly; and the Collector shall a cause notice to be published in the prescribed manner."

6. The learned Advocate has also cited 12 DLR 266 (Saifuddin Kul alias Safiruddin-vs-Moslem Ali Howlader and others) wherein it has been held, inter alia, Sub-section 2 of Section 87 B.T. Act expressly provides that, although in the case of voluntary abandonment of residence, the landlord may enter on the holding and let it out to another tenant or take it into cultivation under himself, yet before he does that, he must file a notice in the prescribed from in the collectors office saying that he has treated the holdings as abandoned and is about to enter on it accordingly, and the collector shall cause the notice to be published in the prescribed manner. In the same decision it has further been held:-

"The Bengal Tenancy Act has not given any definition of the word 'abandonment'. But it connotes the idea of a tenant vacating the land with the intention of never returning to it. Mere temporary absence or absence in circumstances which cannot lead to the inference that the tenant had departed from the land without caring as to what hap-pens thereto, this is not sufficient to warrant the inference of abandonment. It was, therefore, necessary to see some more positive acts than mere non-residence to establish abandonment"

7. On the basis of the aforesaid provision of law the High Court Division has found that alleged abandonment of the suit land by its tenant Gobinda Bairagi could not be established by the plaintiff and making it khash by the landlord in accordance with law. S.A. Khatian admittedly was prepared in the name of Gobinda Bairagi, therefore, it supports that Gobinda Bairagi did not abandon the suit property and the High Court Division did not believe the contention of the plaintiff that landlord made the land khash and took it under his own possession. Further, the High Court Division has held that address of Gobinda Bairagi at 24, parganas of west Bengal in the S.A. khatian cannot take away his right from the suit property, as abandonment by him could not be established. Record of rights in the case reflects the correct state of affairs and reliance has been placed by the High Court Division in decision reported 9 DLR 467.

8. The claim of the plaintiff that he took oral settlement of the suit land. The High Court Division has held that termination of tenancy of Gobinda Bairagi was not made legally. Therefore, whether the settlement was made orally or not is of little significance. In fact, it has no value in the eye of law. Further, the High Court Division has held that proceedings or Rent Suit No. 150 of 1959 has also no impact upon the claim of the plaintiff since it did not reach finality. The High Court Division has held that the defendant admittedly is in possession of the suit land having his huts and homestead on it, It has been held in the case of Lal Miah vs. Hazi Md. Ibrahim reported in 28 DLR 61 that:-

"It well settled that when a defendant is in possession he could be evicted only by a person having a better title over suit land."

9. Further, the High Court Division has held that correctness and genuineness of the deed of purchase of the defendant can be presumed rightly under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act and the plaintiff has failed to rebut the same.

<u>10. Before the High. Court Division plaintiff-opposite party referred to the decision reported in 1 DLR (PC) 5 Hurbert James -vs-Golam Hossain Akeema. The High Court Division found that the said decision is not applicable in the present case because the same does not tally either in spirit of facts. Further, the learned Advocate for the appellant submitted that the appellant filed a Criminal Case against the respondent for disturbing his possession under Section 424/448 which proved appellant's possession in the suit land. It appears that the said Criminal Cass was withdrawn. Therefore, the said case has not bearing upon the decision of the present case. Further, it has been held in the case reported in 3 BLD (AD) 334 that finding of Criminal Courts is not binding on the Civil Courts. The High Court Division has gone to say that the important thing in this case is that the defendant is in possession of the suit land and constructed homestead on the basis of the approved plan from the Municipality and unless the plaintiff can prove, better title he cannot get a decree for declaration of his title and for khas possession. The High Court Division has held that the appellate court upon misreading and non-reading of the evidence on record found the possession in favor of the plaintiff and also found that the defendant had dispossessed him. The High Court Division further accepted the view of the trial Court wherein it has been found that since the termination of tenancy of Gobinda Bairagi by his landlord Ambika Charm could not be proved to have been made in accordance with law the plaintiff's title of the suit land falls like pack of cards having no evidentiary value, Further, the High Court Division has held that the plaintiff can only succeed on the material of his own cause and he cannot get a decree on the weakness or failure of the defendants. This view gets support from the decision in the case of Naimuddin Sarder-vs- Abul Kalam reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237.</u>

11. For the aforesaid reasons the High Court Division has interfered with the judgment and decree of the appellate court which is not sustainable in law, and the Rue) was made absolute. The judgment and decree of the appellate court has been set aside and those of the trial court are restored. The plaintiff's suit has been dismissed.

12. The plaintiff being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order passed by the High Court Division moved this Court and obtained the leave mainly on the grounds that the High Court Division failed to consider properly Ext. 2, suit register of Rent Suit No. 150 of 1956 which proves that landlord Manindra admitted Rakhal as the korfa tenant of the suit land by filing the said rent suit and also Ext.3, the enquiry report of the local Tashilder, in Miscellaneous Case No. 32 of 1968-98 under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950, and Ext. 6 an order of the local circle officer (revenue), for mutating the name of Rakhal on the basis of Ext.3. Further, the High Court Division ought not to have reversed the finding of facts arrived at by the lower appellate Court as to the possession of the parties in the suit land.

13. Plaintiff's Case, in short, is that Gobinda Bairagi died unmarried leaving no heirs, that the landlord took the suit land into his own possession and subsequently, landlord died leaving a son Monindra, who gave oral settlement thereof to Rakhal Chandra, and that the principal defendant dispossessed Rakhal Chandra by Creating a false sale deed.

14. Case of the principal defendant No. 1 is that the said deed is not a false one and that Gobinda Bairagi died leaving a son, Bishweshar Bairagi, who subsequently sold the suit land to the principal defendant No. 1 by the said sale deed in question dated 18.10.1997. The trial Court dismissed the suit. But in appeal the lower appellate Court decreed the suit. Then the principal defendant No. 1 obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 914 of 1987 from the High Court Division, who by the judgment and order dated 26.4.1995 made the Rule absolute and restored the Judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

15. It appears that the plaintiff's claim is that he took oral settlement of the suit land from Monindra but the plaintiff has failed to adduce any paper with regard to the settlement although he has stated that he lost the papers during the liberation war. The basis of alleged oral settlement has not been substantiated by the plaintiff. Further, the Gobinda Bairagi was admittedly the tenant under the landlord Ambika, who did not take the suit land from the aforesaid Gobinda Bairagi legally who could take it under his possession only in compliance of section 87(1)(2) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Therefore, the alleged claim of the plaintiff of no substance since the Gobinda Bairagi never abandoned the suit land and the landlord never took the land in compliance with Section 87(1) & (2) of B.T. Act.

<u>16. There is no doubt that the plaintiff has to prove his own case in order to get the decree in his favour. The plaintiff appellant having failed to substantiate his case of oral settlement by evidence is not entitled to get the decree as prayed for. It has been held in the case of Naimuddin Sander vs. Abul Kalam reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237 that the plaintiff cannot get the decree on the weakness or failure of the defendants to prove his defence. Further, if also appears that S.A. Khatian admittedly stands in the name of Gobinda Bairagi; therefore, it supports the case of the defendant that Gobinda Bairagi did not abandon the suit property and it belies the contention of the plaintiff that land-lord made the land khas and took under his own possession; proceeding of Rent Suit No. 150 of 1959 has also no impact upon the claim of the plaintiff since it did not reach finality. The appellate Court relying on two documents, namely, a certificate from the local Chairman marked Ext. X and the voter list of the locality, which was filed before the appellate Court and found that Gobinda Bairagi was unmarried and Bisheshwar was not his son. The said two documents were not legally proved before the Court in accordance with the provision of order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil procedure. The question of acceptance of the same and the finding on the basis of those documents that Gobinda Bairagi was unmarried and Bisheswar was not his son is not at all legally Correct. Therefore, the High Court Division has correctly reversed the finding of the trial court since it is contrary to evidence on record. The finding is based on inadmissible evidence.</u>

17. Since the plaintiff failed to prove the question of settlement in his favour and since the landlord did not take the suit land in compliance with the provision of section 87(1) of the B.T. Act, the question of finding of possession in favor of the plaintiff does not arise. Gobinda Bairagi was the tenant under superior landlord Ambika Charms and the plaintiff has failed to dismantle the ease of Gobinda Bairagi.

18. The High Court Division has correctly interfered with the judgment and decree of the appellate court; since the plaintiff has felled to prove his case, he is not entitled to decree as prayed for. The High Court Division has rightly reversed the judgment passed by the appellate Court, and restored those of the trial Court.

19. The judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is a elaborate and speaking one, and we are not inclined to interfere With the same.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

The suit has rightly been dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 29.05.2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1360 of 2001.)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin J.: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 29.05.2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1360 of 2001 making the Rule absolute with costs and vacating the order of injunction granted on 29.01.2002 reversing the judgment and decree dated 10.09.2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Rangpur in Other Class Appeal No.77 of 1998 and restoring the judgment and decree dated 29.03.1998 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Mithapukur, Rangpur in Other Class Appeal No.20 of 1989.

2. The facts, in short, are that Badia Sheikh is the original owner of the schedule land measuring 2.27 decimals under C.S Khatian No.354 corresponding to hal khatian No.479 and J.L. No.225 and of survey settlement was prepared and finally published in his name and accordingly he was enjoying the schedule land peacefully without May hindrance from any quarter, that C.S. tenant Badia Sheikh died leaving behind one son, Bhula Sheikh, one wife, Nasiran and two daughters namely, Paglimai and Rahiman Nessa and thereafter wife of Badia Sheikh died leaving behind her aforesaid son and daughters, who are the absolute sharers of the schedule property.

3. Bhula Sheikh, son of Sadia Sheikh sold out 90 decimals of land from C.S. Plot No.1609, 1611 and 1624 of the schedule to the plaintiff and his sister-in-law Rahiman Nessa on 21.12.1953 being sale deed No.23725 and delivered vacant possession to them on the same date and accordingly the father of the plaintiffs Dr. Moslemuddin acquired right, title and interest to the said 45 decimals of land from the aforesaid plot. Subsequently Bhula Sheikh sold out 29 decimals of land from C.S. Plot No.1149 of the schedule to the aforesaid purchasers on 25.11.1954 by sale deed being 15314 and taking over delivery of possession of the aforesaid land they were enjoying the same jointly.

4. Thereafter Rahiman Nessa died leaving behind husband Asimuddin, two sons namely, Md. Tasimuddin and Md. Aziz and one daughter Most. Nurjahan Bibi. Md. Tazimuddin sold out 29 decimals of land from plot No.1609 to Dr. Moslemuddin, predecessor of plaintiffs on 12.01.1968 by sale deed being No.1178 and delivered vacant possession to him on the same day. It is stated that out of aforesaid 29 decimals land. 23½ decimals of land stands as per sahana of Bhula Sheikh. From the above it appears that from Bhula Sheikh, son of C.S. tenant Dr. Moslehuddin and Rahiman Nessa jointly purchased in all 113½ decimals from plot No.1609, 1611, 1624 and 1149 by registered sale deeds being Noa. 23726 dated 23.12.1953 and 153,14 dated 25.11.1954 out of which Dr. Moslemuddin is entitled half of 113½ decimals from only son of Rahiman Nessa from C.S. plot No.1609 by registered sale deed No.1178 dated 12.11.1968 and accordingly he acquired right, title and interest of 80¼ decimals in all our of which 31 decimals of land were sold out and as such Dr. Moslemuddin predecessor of the plaintiffs prayed for partition of his remaining portion, he was dispossessed from 11 decimals of land by defendant Nos.16-20 who constructed pucca structure thereon and as such he also prayed for recovery of khas possession.

5. The defendant Nos.16-18 contested the suit by filing written statement to the effect that the suit is not maintainable in this form and defect of parties and barred by limitation and also stated that Bhula Sheikh was the original C.S. tenant who died leaving one wife, one son and two daughters and as such his son, Bhula Sheikh 1.13½ daughters 55¼ decimals of land got as sharer and accordingly record was prepared and; published in their names and in the meantime Rahiman Nessa died leaving her husband (defendant No.1) two sons (defendant Nos.2-3) and one daughter (defendant No.4) and they amicable made partition among them. Defendant Nos. 1-3 got half of the land from C.S. plot No.1609. Asimuddin and defendant No.3 sold out 0.06 acre and 0.00 acre from plot No.1609 of disputed jote to the defendant Nos.16-18 on 10.12.1983 and 22.06.1982 by registered sale deed and subsequently the defendant Nos.16-18 purchased 0.03 acre of land from plaintiffs from plot No. 609 which was purchased by the plaintiff from Bhula Sheikh and accordingly the defendants acquired right, tide and interest to 0.10 acre of land from disputed plot No. 1609 and defendants have been enjoying the property for about 9 years. The plaintiffs sold out the land to the different persons including the defendants and as such the plaintiffs have no land of 58½ decimals in the suit plot. The other purchasers would be the necessary parties in the suit.

6. Defendant Nos.19 and 20 contested the suit by filing written statement wherein they stated that plaintiff did not purchase 0.33 acre of land from Tajim Uddin or he did not take possession of the same and if so the deed will be the forged and without consideration and accordingly the plaintiff did not get the saham of 0.33 decimals of land. The plaintiff sold out the land to the different person and as such 0¼ decimal of land of the disputed jote may be remained with him. On the other hand defendant No.29 contested the suit by filing written statements wherein he stated that from disputed jote Ehula Sheikh 1.13½ acre and Rahiman Nessa including Paglaimai each of the .56¼ decimal of land got as saham and they enjoyed the same jointly and accordingly C.S: and S.A. records were rightly prepared as their saham. Rahiman Nessa sold out some portion of land and after death of Rahiman Nessa her husband Azimuddin got one anna, two sons, defendant Nos.2-3 namely, Abdul Aziz and Tajimuddin each of them got /22/5 pai and one daughter, defendant No.4 Nurjahan got /21/5 pai as their saham. They possessed land of disputed jote and on amicable partition defendant Abdul Aziz sold out 0.3½ acre from plot No.1609 and 1/2 acre from plot No.1612 to the defendant by registered sale deed being No.1791 dated 17.01.1983 and the defendant took possession and is enjoying the same. Lastly the defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing the written statement wherein it is stated that defendant Nos.1-3 were the heirs of Rahiman Nessa, out of them defendant No.2 sold out his share of 0.24 decimals of land from plot Nos.1609, 1611 and 1624 to one Zahura on 06.08.1978 who sold out the same to Sarwar Hussain, son of defendant No.2 on 19.10.1978. Paglimai Bibi, mother of defendant No.5 transfers .23½ acre of land from disputed plot No.1149 and 1609 to Musammat Sarwan Nessa, wife of defendant No.2 on 26.01.1981 by heba bil ewaj deed No.2356 and surrendered the possession of the land. The defendant No.2 had no right to sale the land and he did not sale 0.33 acre of land to the plaintiff by kabala No.1178 dated 12.01.1968 and if so, he created the said deed by applying fraud, beyond the knowledge of defendant No.2.

7. The trial court dismissed the suit on appeal the judgment of the trial court was set aside and the suit was sent back on remand to amend the plaint with prayer for recovery of khas possession in respect of 11 decimals of land from which the plaintiff was dispossessed and thereafter the plaintiff amended the plaint and ultimately after hearing the trial court decreed the suit and the defendant preferred appeal before the learned District Judge and again the appellate court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court.

8.The plaintiff then preferred Civil Revision No.1360 of 2001 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division after hearing parties made the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment of the appellate court.

9. As against the judgment of the High Court Division the defendant petitioners have filed this petitioner for leave to appeal.

10. Heard the learned Advocate and perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other papers on record.

<u>11. It appears that the High Court Division found that the appellate court did not consider the evidence on record while setting aside the judgment of the trial court and further held that the plaintiffs kabala was earlier ion the basis of which they took possession from the admitted co sharer and the defendants are subsequent purchaser from the plaintiff as well as the co-sharers and they cannot deny the title and possession of the plaintiff.</u>

<u>12. We do not find any substance in this petition which is accordingly dismissed.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to appeal No. 556 of 2006
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Senior Advocate, instructed by Bivash Chandra Biswas, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners 
For the Respondents ------ Not Represented
parties:
Palash Kumar Saha and another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Santosh Chandra Roy and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25.10.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 243 of 1987)
full_judgment:
Md. Joynul Abedin J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 25.10.2005 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 243 of 1987 discharging the rule.

2. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit jama appertains 25 decimals of land originally belonged to Banomali Das to the extent of eight anas share, Ramesh Chandra Das to the extent of four annas share, Harendra Nath Das and Babu Rain Das to the extent of two anas each banomali Das died leaving behind three sons defendant No.1, Surendra Chandra. The defendant no. 2, Taruni Chandra and Ramesh Chandra Ramesh Chandra died leaving behind his brother Surandra Chandra and Taruni Chandra as his heirs. The another co-share recorded tenant Ramesh Chandra also died leaving behind his son Manoj Kumar Das, the defendant No.3; Babu Rain died leaving behind two sons, Manindra Nath Das, the defendant No.8, and Fanindra Nath Das. Fanindra died unmarried and as such his share devolved upon his full brother, the defendant No.8. Harandra Nath Das died leaving behind his widow Charubala Das who inherited his share. There exists a path way in the middle of the suit plot stretching north-south and is about 4 cubit in measurement in width. The defendants Nos. 1-3 are possessing the northern part of the suit plot for a period of more than 25-26 years. The defendant Nos. 1-3 sold out some portion of their share to the defendant Nos. 4,5 and 6 Charubala, the widow of Harendra Nath sold out her entire share to the defendant No.7 and delivered possession. The defendant No.8, Manindra has sold out 4½ decimals of land to the plaintiff by a registered deed of kabala dated 25.2.1975 and delivered possession. The plaintiff has been possessing the land since the date of kabala. But in the middle of Ashhin 1384 Bangla Shal, the defendant No.1 in collusion with the defendant Nos. 2-3 and at the instance of the defendant No.6 enclosed insider the land of the plaintiff and constructed a chala ghar and thus illegally dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land and the defendants refused to remove those chala ghar from the suit land and hence the suit.

<u>3. The defendant No.7 entered appearance and filed an application for separate saham contending, inter alia, that the recorded tenant Harendra Nath Das having his share to the extent of two anas, died leaving behind his only widow Charubala. And this defendant has purchased the entire two anas share measuring 5 decimals of land from Charubala, the said widow of Harendra Nath by registered deed of kabala dated 8.3.1975 at appropriate consideration. Charubala delivered possession to the defendant No. 7 who constructed dwelling house from south-west corner of the plot in question and has been possessing by paying rent to the Government since purchase and as such the defendant No.7 is praying for separate saham in respect of the said land.</u>

<u>4. The defendant Nos. 1-4 have contested the suit by filing joint written statement denying all the material allegation as set forth in the plaint. The case of the defendant Nos. 1-4, in short, is that Banamali was the owner to the extent of eight anas share, Ramesh Chandra Das was the owner to the extent of four anas share and Harendra Bath and Babu Rain Das were the owner to the extent of two anas share in each of the plot in question as it was stated in the plaint. There is a path way dividing the plot in the middle extending to north south for easy movement of the co-sharers. The defendant No.1 as the heir of Banamali is possessing the share of Banamali from the northern side of the plot, both sides of the path way. The defendant No.3 Monoj Kumar, the son of the recorded tenant Ramesh Chandra sold out his share to the defendant Nos. 5-6. The defendant No.6 sold out his purchased land to Faku Ram. The defendant No.8, the heir of the recorded tenant Babu Ram Das and the defendant No.5 have been possessing their respective share. The defendant Banamali died leaving behind three sons, Surendra Nath Das, the defendant No.1, Taruni Chandra Das, the defendant No.2 and Ramesh Chandra Das. The recorded tenant Ramesh Chandra died leaving behind his son Manoj Kumar Das, the defendant No.3. The defendant Nos. 1-3 have got right, title and possession to the extent of two anas eight pies. The recorded tenant Ramesh Chandra Das died his four anas share was inherited by the defendant Nos. 1-3, Harendra Nath Das and Babu Ram Das. The defendant Nos. 1-3 have got share together to the extent of one ana four pies share from Ramesh Chandra while Harendra Nath and Babu Ram have got the share to the extent of one ana four pies from Ramesh Chandra. The defendant Nos. 1-3 have got the share to the extent of one ana four pies from Ramesh Chandra while Harendra Nath and Babu Ram have got the share to the extent of 5-1/3 pies each from Ramesh Chandra. Harendra Nath Das became the owner of the share to the extent of 2 anas + 1 ana 4 pies = 3 anas 4 pies. Harendra died leaving behind two paternal Uncle's son, the defendant Nos. 1-2 and one widow Charubala who has got life interest in the property left by her husband. Thereafter Charubala died and as such, the defendant Nos. 1-2 have inherited Harendra having share to the extent of 1 ana 8 pies each left by Harendra. Thus the defendant Nos. 1-2 have got the share to the extent of 2 anas 8 pies + 5-1/3 pies + 1 ana 8 pies = 4 anas 9-1/3 pies each from the said jama. Taruni Chandra Das, the defendant No.2 died leaving behind his full brother, the defendant No.1 to inherit him. Thus the defendant No.1 became the owner of 9 anas 6-2/3 pies. The defendant No.1 has sold out 2½ decimals of land through two deeds of kabala to the defendant No.4 and delivered possession. Thereafter Surendra Nath died leaving behind three sons and one widow, the defendant Nos. 1- 1(Ga), who arc the owner of 12½ decimals of land deducting the sold property measuring 2½ decimals of land in favour of the defendant No.4 and these defendants are praying for separate saham.</u>

5. The defendant No.5 has prayed for separate saham contending, inter alia, that the defendant No.3 sold out 1½ decimals of land to the defendant No. 5 by registered deed of kabala dated 2.8.1975 and delivered possession. By constructing dwelling house, this defendant is residing therein.

<u>6. The learned trial Judge while trying the suit framed as many as seven issues as to whether the suit is maintainable in its present form, whether the suit is barred by limitation and by principle of waiver, estoppels and acquiescence and by principle of adverse possession, whether the suit is valued and stained properly; as to whether the plaintiff has got any right, title and interest over the suit land; whether the suit is bad for defect of parties; whether the plaintiff is entitled to get relief as prayed for and whether the plaintiff is entitled to get any other relief.</u>

7. In course of trial, the plaintiff and the defendants have adduced witnesses in support of their respective claim. The learned trial judge upon careful consideration of all the evidence both oral and documentary and other materials on record passed the judgment and decree dated 23.2.1984 granting saham to all the parties including the plaintiff. The learned trial Judge found that the defendant No. 7 has got right, title and possession over 5 decimals of land as such he would get saham in respect of the same.

8. The defendant No.1 being dissatisfied preferred Title Appeal No. 28 of 1985 before the learned District Judge, Bogra. On transfer, the same was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Bogra who by taking erroneous view affirmed the judgment and decree as passed by the trial court in part, with modification. The lower appellate court found that the defendant No.7 has got no right, title and interest in the suit jama because he could not prove that Charubala due to her legal necessity transferred the property by the registered deed of kabala dated 8.3.1975 to defendant No. 7 and as such he will not get any saham. It was also found that the defendant Nos. 3-8 will not be entitled to get any saham.

9. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant No.7 preferred Civil Revision No. 243 of 1987 in the High Court Division. After hearing the High Court Division discharged the rule. Thereafter being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the High Court Division the petitioner filed this civil petition for leave to appeal.

10. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner submits that kabala deed dated 8.3.1975 duly executed and registered by Charubala, marked as exhibit A-1, the recital of which is the best evidence of legal necessity for alienation which clearly shows that for the purpose of Sraddhya and for offering pindi at Gaya of her deceased husband Harendra Chandra Das, such alienation took place, non-consideration of such factual and legal proposition led the single Judge of the High Court Division to commit error in law which resulted in miscarriage of justice. He lastly submits that admittedly the suit is brought for the relief for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession against the defendant Nos. 1-3 and for partition. No allegation against the kabala dated 8.3.1975, the exhibit mark A-1, was raised by either party to the suit. And as such the alienation was made by Charubala on the ground of legal necessity as it is evident from the recital of exhibit A-1 and the same not being controverter the single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in not granting saham in favour of the petitioner, the heirs of the defendant No.7, which has resulted in miscarriage of justice.

11. We have heard the learned Advocate and perused the connected papers including the impugned judgment. We do not find any substance in the points raised. The High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record has arrived at a correct decision. We therefore find no interference with the same.

12. Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: - This appeal by leave, is against the judgment and order dated March 27, 1997 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 7646 of 1991 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated February 19, 1991 of the Court of District Judge, Jessore, in Title Appeal No. 92 of 1987 allowing the appeal and thereupon dismissing the suit. The appeal was filed against the judgment and decree dated September 2, 1985 of the Court of Munsif (Now Assistant Judge), Minirampur Upazilla, Jessore, passed in Title Suit No. 19 of 1984 decreeing the same. The suit was filed for declaration of title and for confirmation of possession in the land described in the schedule.

2. The plaintiff-Respondent Nos. 1-10 filed the suit stating, inter alia, that the land in suit measuring 4.08 acres of C.S. Khatian No. 876 corresponding to S.A. Khatian No. 1 of Monza Machine belonged to Dhirendra Nath Roy, Zamindar of Nandi Zamindari Estate, that the Zamindar orally settled the land to the plaintiffs on 20th Poush, 1354 B.S. and since then plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit. It was also the case of the plaintiffs that the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 claimed title in the land in suit in the month of Bhadra, 1383 B.S. disclosing that they have taken settlement from the Government and then on enquiry plaintiffs came to know from the local thesis office that the land in suit has been incorrectly recorded in S.A. Khatian in the name of the Government and the said wrong recording having had clouted plaintiffs' title they were constrained to file the suit seeking declaration of title and confirmation of possession.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 1, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh by filling written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the land in suit was retainable khas land of the Zamindar and  that the land in suit with other non-retainable lands of the Zamindar vested with the Government as per provision of section 20(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and that during S.A. survey operation the land was correctly recorded in the khas khatian No. 1 in the name of the Government and that the Government has given permanent lease to different persons on different dates and the lessees are in possession of the land in suit. It was also the case of the contesting defendant that the plaintiffs by creating forged and ante-dated documents want to grab the land in suit.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the  evidence brought on record by the parties decreed the suit on the finding that though the plaintiffs failed to produce documentary evidence in support of their claim in respect of the land in suit but they are in possession of the land in suit and that although the defendant claimed that the land in suit has been settled to different persons and the lessees of the defendant are in possession but the defendant failed to produce evidence before the Court in support of the said claim and that from the evidence of the plaintiffs' witnesses it is seen that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their case.

5. It may be mentioned that discussion of the evidence made by the trial Court is not of the kind as ought to have been by the first Court of fact.

6. The contesting defendant went on appeal. The appellate Court noticed that the contesting defendant in support of its claim that the land in suit was the non-retainable land of  the Zamindar and the same was acquired as per provision of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not file any paper relating to preparation of compensation assessment roll and compensation, if any, paid to the ex-zamindar or that compensation was assessed but the zamindar did not withdraw the same in spite of payment and thereupon  observed "In the absence of the same it is very much hard to believe the defence contention that the suit lands have been duly acquired by the Government under section 20(2) of the S.A. non & T. Act, as non-retainable khas properties of the admitted ex-zamihdar". The appellate Court also observed that although contesting defendant claimed that the land in suit has been leased out by the Government and the same is possessed by the lessees on the basis of the registered kabuliyat which were produced before the trial Court and were marked as Exts. but later on the same were taken back and were not produced before the appellate Court and as such adverse presumption in the light of the provision of section 114(h) of the Evidence Act can very much be drawn as to the genuineness of the said documents and the lessees, as claimed by the defendant, are not witness in the case in support of the claim of the defendant that the lessees are in possession of the land in suit. In the background of the aforesaid observations the appellate Court held the Government has failed to prove that the suit lands were nonreturnable khas lands of the ex-zamindar of Narail and Government acquired the same under section 20(2)of the S.A. & T. Act and since then it has been possessing through its lessees".

7. The appellate Court after making the aforesaid finding and decision considered the case of the plaintiffs and observed, "So the story of pattern found to have not been proved beyond reasonable doubt".

8. The P. W. 1, one of the plaintiffs, while deposing in support of plaintiffs' claim of taking settlement of the land in suit stated that at the time of taking pattan Mongal Gazi, Syed Ali, Shahadat, Obaidullah and Hussain Sardar were present but the plaintiffs for the purpose of corroborating P.W. 1 so far his evidence relating to pattan did not examine none of the persons claimed to have been present at the time of pattan but examined P.Ws. 2 and 3 who were not the persons, as mentioned by P.W.1, present at the time of paten. It may also be mentioned no explanation was offered by the plaintiffs for non-examination of the persons who, as being ready for claimed by the P.W.1, were present at the time of pattan. The appellate Court in the afore state of the matter placed no reliance on the P.Ws. 2 and 3 who were examined to corroborate the P.W. 1 as regard the matter of pattan.

9. It was the case of the plaintiffs that talk of the pattan took place with the Manager of the Zamindar. In that background the appellate Court observed that no material was brought on record to show that the Manager of the ex- zamindar was competent to settle the land and that no material was also brought on record, that at the time of talk of pattan Zamindar was present or consented to the pattan or received the salami. The appellate Court also noticed that dakhilas produced by the plaintiffs in support of their case of taking pattan of the land in suit do not bear the signature of the Manager who, as claimed by the plaintiffs settled the land, that the scribe of the plaintiffs settled the land, that the scribe of the dakhilas i.e. Naib of the ex-zamindar was not examined and for such non- examination no explanation was offered. On examination and scrutiny of the dakhilas the appellate Court arrived at the finding "The dakhilas Ext.1 series found to have been made old by artificial means and the close scrutiny of the same clearly indicates that the same were written in one sitting by an in-experienced hand  The Ext.1 series in no way inspire confidence about its age as shown thereto", and the claim of the P.Ws.2 and 3 of their being present at the time of pattan can not be accepted since P. W.1 has not stated about the presence of the said witnesses at the time of taking pattan; by the plaintiffs and that the said witnesses "failed to prove the particulars of the dakhilas Ext. 1 series". In the afore state of the matter the appellate Court arrived at the finding "I do not find any reason to believe that they (EWs.2-3) were present at the time of granting the dakhilas Ext. 1 series or their presence at the time of alleged Inman- or that the same i.e. pattan had actually taken place.

10. The dakhilas Ext. 1 series filed by the plaintiffs also do not create much confidence. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances; I am constrained to hold that the story of patan is a mere myth and the dakhilas Ext. 1 series are mere paper transaction and no reliance can be reposed on them. The evidence of possession of the plaintiffs is also found unsatisfactory". Plaintiffs other then P.W.1 examined P.ws. 2 and 3 to prove their claim of possession in the land in suit. The appellate Court on consideration of the evidence of the said witnesses (P.Ws. 2 and 3) arrived at the finding that evidence of record clearly shows that the said P.Ws, do not know the suit land. The appellate Court on consideration of the evidence produced by the plaintiffs in support of their claim of taking pattan of the land in suit has observed" the facts and circumstances so discussed above clearly indicates that the story of pattan of the plaintiffs is not true and the papers (Ext. 1 series) so filed on this behalf are found nothing but forged, collusive, ante-dated and created for the purpose of this suit". The appellate Court has held that the plaintiffs have not acquired title in the land in suit by lapse of time since they had no case in their pleading as regard acquiring title by lapse of time and that no evidence was also led from the plaintiffs' side as regard the case of acquiring title of the land in suit by lapse of time. On the aforesaid findings and decision the appellate Court allowed the appeal and thereupon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court dismissed the suit.

11. The plaintiffs moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing that the plaintiffs in support of their case of taking settlement of the land in suit produced the rent receipts Ext. 1 series and has proved possession in the land in suit and the Government in support of its case that its lessees are in possession of the land in suit did not examine any one of the lessees and the Government in support of its case that the land in suit being the non-retainable land of the Zamindar was acquired by the Government did not produce the compensation assessment roll.

12. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute placed reliance on some of the observations as to the case of the respective parties made by the appellate Court and in the background of the said observations, as stated hereinbefore, the High Court Division held that the appellate Court was in error in reversing the judgment of the trial Court. As to the genuineness of the Ext.1 series the High Court Division has observed, The trial Court found the rent receipts, Ext. 1 series, to be genuine. I myself also examined the rent receipts which is in a printed form and same appears to be genuine". On the point as regard the question of possession of the parties in the land in suit the High Court Division has observed that the Government failed to prove their possession by producing their lessees and thereupon observed "Thus I find that the trial Court has rightly decreed the suit".

13. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the High Court Division was in error in setting aside the finding of fact arrived at by the Court of appeal below which is the final Court of fact upon shifting the onus on the defendants and that in the absence of legal infirmity in the finding of fad arrived at by the Court of appeal below in respect of settlement and possession High Court Division exceeded its jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in making the Rule absolute and setting aside the judgment of the Court of appeal below.

14. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division was of the view that the trial Court discussed the evidence while decreeing the suit "but the appellate Court did not properly discussed witness".

15. On our perusal of the judgment of the trial Court, as has already been observed hereinbefore, that the said Court as the initial Court of fact in fact did not discuss the evidence as the law enjoins.

16. The appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court has rejected the evidence of P.Ws.2 and 3 who examined from the side of the plaintiffs to corroborate the P.W.1 as regard the case of taking pattan of the land from the Ex-zamindar since the said P.Ws. were not the persons whom the P.W.1 stated were present at the time of pattan. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute did not reverse the reasoning and the finding given by the appellate Court in rejecting the evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3.

<u>17. The law is well settled that the extent of jurisdiction of the revisional Court is limited. The revisional Court is within its jurisdiction in reversing the judgment of the lower Court if the same is the result of misreading of the evidence or has been made leaving the legal evidence out of consideration or that while arriving at the decision misconstrued the documentary evidence or left the vital evidence out of consideration without assigning any reason. If the judgment of the lower Court does not suffer from any one of the aforesaid defects the revisional court is not competent to disturb the finding and decision arrived at by the last Court of fact. In the instant case it is seen from the judgment of the appellate Court that the said Court on examination of the documents (Ext. 1 series) arrived at the finding that those are not genuine. The High Court Division did arrived at the finding that the finding so made by the appellate Court was made upon misreading of the evidence or non-consideration of the evidence. The High Court Division without reversing the finding of the appellate Court on the nature and character of the dakhilas (Ext.1 series) exceeded its revisional jurisdiction in disturbing the finding of the appellate Court as regard the genuineness of the dakhilas. Since from the plaintiffs' side no case of misreading or non-consideration of the evidence was made out before the High Court Division as regard the finding arrived at by the appellate Court as to the quality of the Ext.1 series or in other words genuineness of the said Ext. 1 series the said Division erred in re-assessing the evidence as to Ext. 1 series and thereupon disturbing the finding of the last Court of fact as regard the Ext.1 series. It appears the High Court Division based its judgment on certain observations made by the appellate Court as to the infirmity in the case of the defendant and that as to the steps taken by the plaintiffs in proof of its case. The High Court Division while setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court did not at all address itself to the material findings arrived at by the said Court on the question of taking settlement of the land in suit as claimed by the plaintiffs, nature and quality of the dakhilas produced by the plaintiffs in support of their claim of taking settlement of the land in suit, effect of non-examination of the scribe of the dakhilas and that absence of evidence from the side of the plaintiffs as to that Zamindar consented to the pattan and accepted salami and finally finding of the appellate Court as regard possession in the and in suit by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs examining P.W.1 in support of their claim of taking pattan of the land in suit and examined the P.Ws. 2 and 3 for the purpose of corroboration of the evidence of P.W.1 on the point of taking pattan of the land in suit by the plaintiffs. The appellate court upon assigning due reasoning rejected the evidence of P.Ws.2 and 3. It may be mentioned the High Court Division has not reversed the finding of the appellate Court relating to discarding the evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3. The High Court Division overlooked the material fact that there was no reliable evidence to corroborate the evidence of P.W. 1 as regard the material fact of settling the land by the Zamindar to the plaintiffs. The appellate Court discarded the evidence of P.Ws.2 and 3 on the question of possession of the land in suit by the plaintiffs. This finding of the appellate Court was also not reversed by the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute.</u>

18. In the afore state of the matter we are of the view that the High Court Division was in serious error in disturbing the finding of fact arrived at by the appellate Court when the said Division did not hold that the finding and decision made by the appellate Court was vitiated by non-consideration of the evidence or misreading of evidence or that the appellate Court left the vital evidence out of consideration for no valid reason while making its decision on the question of taking pattan of the land in suit by the plaintiffs and the nature and character of the Ext.1 series as well as regarding possession of the plaintiffs.

19. In the background of the discussions made hereinabove we are of the view the appeal has merit.

Accordingly the appeal is allowed with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin J.:- This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 27.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 114 of 1996 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 27.04.1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 309 of 1994 dismissing the suit. 

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.309 of 1994 contending, inter-alia, that the plaintiffs (the present petitioner) are entitled to a decree declaring their entitlement to get an offer from the defendants to sell the scheduled abandoned property under the Government circular/policy as being a valid allotted in possession. 

3. The suit property originally belonged to the then Government of East Pakistan which was subsequently-, leased out to a Non-Bengali refugee. After 1971 the said Non-Bengali refugee was not found in the suit property known as 1/3, Noorjahan Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. Therefore by operation of the President Order 16 of 1972 it was declared as an. abandoned property and it was listed as an abandoned property. The suit property was then allotted to the father/husband of the plaintiffs, Mr. Sona Miah, a Police Habilder serving under the Government of Bangladesh, by allotment letter dated 03.02.1973 and handed over possession on 05.02.1973. The said allottee Mr. Sona Miah paid rent for suit property firstly 71/2 and then 5% of his salary as a Police Habilder as per the demand note dated 15.05.1975 issued by the defendants. 

4. The said allottee, Sona Miah, had been living in the suit property with his family members including the plaintiffs only and he had been paying rent for the suit property regularly from his salary until lie retired from the Government service 1982. Thereafter, Sona Miah tried to pay the rent from the pension allowance he received from the Government but the defendants refused to take rent. 

5. The predecessor of the plaintiffs, Sona Miah, made applications dated 29.06.1994 to the abandoned property authority for an offer of sale of the suit property under the Government circular bearing memo No. Shakha- 5/AP-1M-26/83 (ANG1 SFIA)/110 dated 02.03.1986 but the defendants delayed the offer for a long time with-out giving any answer at the investigation of some corrupt employees and some interested persons who were conspiring to give offer letter to another person. On 30.11.1994 the predecessor of the plaintiffs, Sona Miah died leaving behind the plaintiffs. Thereafter the defendants served notice to evict the plaintiffs from the suit property, hence the suit. 

6. The defendant Nos. 1 to 4 and defendant No. 5 filed two separate written statements contending, inter-alia that the suit property was originally allotted to Sona Miah by the defendants and accordingly a demand note was also issued in his name Sona Miah has been in possession with the plaintiffs. 

7. Later on, one Maleka Begum in the name of Sona Miah filed a case in the court of settlement claiming the ownership of the suit property being Settlement Case No. 701 of 1988 which was rejected by the court in the year of 1990 and then filed a writ petition being Writ Petition No. 106 of 1994 in the High Court Division which was also rejected. Thereafter, she filed a Civil Appeal being C.P. No. 181 of 1994 before the Appellate Division which was also rejected. 

8. The suit has been filed by the plaintiff No. 1 Nazrul Islam and the defendant No. 2 Mrs. Feroza Begum but aforesaid Maleka Begum and the said Feroza Begum are the same person. When the said Maleka Begtim failed to get the ownership then she again became Feroza Begum as the widow of the said Sona Miah. 

9. The said suit property was offered for sale to the defendant No. 5 as a Shaheed family.

10. After hearing both the parties, the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka passed the judgment and decree dated 27.04.1996 in Title Suit No. 309 of 1994 dismissing the petitioners' suit on contest. 

11. Being aggrieved by the above judgment and decree the petitioners preferred an appeal being First Appeal No. 114 of 1996 before the High Court Division. After hearing the parties in the said appeal the High Court Division was pleased to pass judgment and order dated 27.01.2009 dismissing the First Appeal No. 114 of 1996. 

12. As against the judgment and order of the High Court Division the petitioners have filed this petition for leave to appeal. 

13. Heard Mr. Tafailur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners and Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents and perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other papers on record. 

14. It appears that the High Court Division found that the trial court rightly held that the petitioners had no right or interest in the suit property and therefore the very suit was not maintainable and the Government never made any offer or expressed its desire to sell the suit property in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiffs predecessor was only an allottee under the Government having no right or interest in the property itself. 

15. In such circumstances the High Court Division committed no illegality in dismissing the appeal. 

16. We find no substance in this petition which is accordingly dismissed. 

End.

full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order No. 12 dated 14-3-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 107 of 1999 rejecting the petition filed by the plaintiff petitioner for holding local investigation.

2. The case of the plaintiff, in brief, is that Jagath Ram Chose purchased the suit land along with other land from its owner Chandra Ram Chose by a kabala of 1318 BS and while owning and possessing he died leaving behind his wife Sushila Sundari as his only heir who while owning and possessing sold out the same for her maintenance and payment of debt in favour of plaintiff's predecessor Basantha Kumar Chose vide registered kabla dated 5th Sraban, 1334 BS and delivered possession thereof; that plaintiff's predecessor continued to hold and possess the same; that Sushila Sundori Chose transferred some other land which was contiguous west of the suit land in favour of Dinonath Chose in the year 1934 and thereafter said Dinonath Ghose transferred the same in favour of plaintiff's father; that the plaintiff inherited the suit land along with other land from his father and while owning and possessing he came to know on 15-6-1998 from defendant No. 2 that the suit land is recorded in the name of defendant No. 1 along with plaintiffs father and that the plaintiff requested the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to execute a deed of relinquishment but they denied to execute the same and then the plaintiffs were constrained to file the suit.

3. Defendant No. 2 filed a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land and other lands belonged to defendant No. 1 Deity and Babu Radha Lal Gupta while administering and possessing the tea garden as shebait and died leaving behind 2 sons namely, Rajendra Lal Gupta and Rabindra Lal Gupta and while they were possessing the land, Pakistani Army killed them at the time of liberation war and that thereafter Pankaj Kumar Gupta while performing as shebait leased out the property of tea garden in favour of defendant No. 2 and since then the defendant No. 2 has been holding and possessing the same. The further defence case is that the deeds mentioned in plaint do not attract the suit land and that the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. While the suit was pending in the trial Court the plaintiff filed a petition on 1-3-2000 for holding local investigation by survey knowing Advocate Commissioner for relaying the suit land with the land of title deeds mentioned in the plaint as in those deeds there was no mention of plot number and khatian number, etc as because those deeds were executed and registered long before the SA operation came into being.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge heard the petition on 14-3-2000 and rejected the same holding that there is no connection of technical determination with the petition for local investigation and that the matter can be resolved by oral evidence.

6. The plaintiff as petitioner has preferred this revision challenging the impugned order No. 12 dated 14-3-2000 and obtained the Rule.

7. The only point for determination whether the judgment and order No. 12 dated 14-3-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Sylhet has committed any error of law resulting in an error in decision occasioning failure of justice.

8. Mr Khijir Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that after filing of the suit in the trial Court, it was detected that there is no mention of plot and khatian in the deeds mentioned in the plaint as the deeds were executed and registered before SA operation; that it is necessary to determine whether the land of deeds in question relates to the suit land for which the plaintiff filed a petition on 1-3-2000 for holding local investigation by an Advocate Commissioner for relaying the suit land with the land of title deeds mentioned in the plaint. He further submits that the defendant in his written statement denied that the deeds of the plaintiffs are not related to suit land but the defendant-respondent admitted to this extent that the suit land could not be properly ascertained and identified without local investigation.

9. No one appears to oppose the Rule.

10. Perused the application and written statement and other materials on record.

11. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for declaration of title in respect of the land of the registered deed of 1318 BS executed by Jagothram in favour of Chandra Ram Ghose and the land of registered deed dated 5th Srabon, 1334 BS executed by Susila Shundori Ghosh in favour of Basanto Kumar Ghosh.

12. There is no denying of the facts that there is no mention of dag and khatian in those kabalas referred to in the plaint as those are executed and registered long before the settlement operation. As the defendant No. 2 stated in paragraph 11(Uma) of the written statement that the suit land does not attract the land of those Kabalas, so the plaintiff filed an application on 1-3-2000 under section 75 read with Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for local investigation for the purpose of relaying the suit land and for elucidating the matter in dispute. But the learned Subordinate Judge heard the petition on 14-3-2000 and rejected the same holding that the matter can be resolved by oral evidence.

13. Now let us discuss the relevant section and order in order to see whether the court has jurisdiction to consider the prayer for local investigation. Section 75 runs thus:

"75 Power of Court to issue commission. Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, the court may issue a commission—

a) to examine any person;

b) to make a local investigation:

c) to examine or adjust account; or

d) to make a partition.

14. Order XXVI, rule 9 runs thus:

"9. Commissions to make a local investigation. In any suit in which the court deems a local investigation to be requisite or proper for the purpose of elucidating in any matter in dispute, or ascertaining the market value of any property, or the amount or any mesne profits or damages or annual net profits, the court may issue a commission to such person as it thinks fit directing him to make such investigation and to report thereon to the court within such time not exceeding three months as may be fixed by the Court.

Provided that the court may on the prayer of the commission and on sufficient cause being shown, extend time."

15. On perusal of the legal position quoted above, it appears that the court has jurisdiction to appoint a commission to make a local investigation for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute. The object of local investigation under Order IX is to obtain evidence which from its peculiar nature can best be had from the spot itself. Such evidence enables the court to properly and correctly understand and assess the evidence on record. It clarifies or explains any point which is left doubtful on the evidence on record. The local investigation pre-supposes the existence on the record of independent evidence which requires to be elucidated. The purpose of local investigation under Order XXVI, rule 9 is ascertaining, collecting or elucidating facts in respect of any matters in dispute after proper scrutiny, examination and collecting of materials.

<u>16. In the instant case, it is urgently necessary to ascertain through local investigation whether the land of registered kabala of 1318 BS and the land of registered kabala dated 5th Srabon, 1334 BS, relates to suit land or not. This fact cannot be collected through oral evidence and this matter can only be ascertained through relayment of the land of kabalas stated in the plaint. It is to be ascertained first, whether the land of the kabalas of the plaintiff attracts the suit land or not. Without relayment, such matter cannot be elucidated because there is no mention of plot and khatian in those kabalas referred to in the plaint as those were executed and registered long before the SA operation came into being.</u>

17. We may profitably refer the decisions reported in the case of Md Belayet Hosain vs Shah Alam Parvez and others 1999 BLD 359 and in the case of Abdur Rahman and others vs Mir Abdul Kuddus and others 4 MLR 281. The decisions of these cases clearly state the substance of Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the effect that if there is any vagueness of the land of any deed, that should be cleared first through relaying the land of the kabala in question with the suit land for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute.

<u>18. The learned Subordinate Judge without going through the facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record simply stated in the impugned judgment that the matter can be resolved through oral evidence. He totally failed to understand the legal position and facts of the case. The learned Subordinate Judge failed to apply his judicial mind in passing the impugned order.</u>

19. For the discussion made above we are of the opinion that the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner merit consideration.

20. In view of the matter, the impugned order appears to be illegal and arbitrary and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

21. In the result, the Rule succeeds and it is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 14-6-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 107 of 1999 rejecting the petition for local investigation is set aside.

22. The order of stay earlier granted by this court stands vacated.

23. The learned Subordinate Judge is directed to make arrangement for promptly holding local investigation by a survey knowing Advocate Commissioner and to conclude the trial of the suit in accordance with law.

24. Communicate at once.

Since this is an old case, it is expedient in the inters of justice that it be disposed of with utmost expediency , preferably within 6(six) months from the date of acceptance of commission's report without granting adjournment to the contending parties except on compelling reasons.

End.
