parties:
Rumana Afrin and  ----- Plaintiff
Vs.
Fakir Ashrafuddin Ahmed & Others ----- Defendants
full_judgment:
Md. Gholam Rabbani J: In this transferred suit plaintiff Rumana Afrin prays for the custody of her two minor daughters and for declaring her as their legal guardian. Her former husband Fakir Ashrafuddin Ahmed is the first defendant. Other defendants are her former in-laws.

2. They were married on 27-6-92. It was a negotiated marriage. First defendant is an immigrant in USA. He married her stating that he was a bachelor. But it transpired later on that he married twice in USA and the second marriage was subsisting when he married the plaintiff.

3. The couple had two daughters out of the wedlock. First daughter Abida Ahmed and second daughter Nomat Ahmed are now aged respectively about three years and two years.

4. Ultimately, the marriage between the parties was dissolved on compromise with effect from 3-8-95. Plaintiff on 21-12-95 handed over the custody of the daughters to the first defendant, but subsequently she filed this suit on 8-4-96. These are the facts necessary for the disposal of the suit and they are not disputed.

Issue

1.	What is the Islamic law of hidnat i.e. guardianship and custody of the minor children?

2.	Has the plaintiff forfeited her right of hidnat by handing over the custody of the daughters to the first defendant?

3.	Is declaring the plaintiff's guardianship to be for the welfare of the minors?

5. Mr. Abdul Hameed Chowdhury, defendants' learned Advocate, at the outset has submitted that the plaintiff's case stands not proved as she did not herself give evidence. Before we discuss the issues we like to answer this point. It is not obligatory for a plaintiff to depose in his or her suit. Order 18, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure prescribes that the parties shall state their case and produce evidence at the hearing, but it does not prescribe that the plaintiff or defendant must depose. There is no adverse presumption within the scope of section 114 of the Evidence Act against the person who does not appear in the court where there are materials on record regarding the point in issue. However, it may so happen that a particular averment in the pleading necessitated examination of the plaintiff or the defendant, then for his non-examination his case may suffer. But the instant suit is not such a case. Herein we have already stated that the facts are not disputed. Issue No. 1.

"Say: Obey God and His Apostle" (3rd Sura Al-I-Imran, Verse 32). By this command Quran established Its legislative authority.

"Narrated Abdullah Ibne Amar Ibne Aas: A woman said to the Prophet (peace be upon him), This is my son—my womb was his vessel, my breast was his water-front and my lap was his cradle. His father has divorced me. Now his father is resolved to take him away from me. Prophet (peace be upon him) said to her, 'you alone have the claim over him till you do not remarry."

This hadith is numbered 2276 in the chapter of 'Book of Divorce' under Vol. II of "Sahih Abu Daud' and is quoted at page 182 of Vol. II of "Musnad-i-Ahmad-ibn Hammal'.

6. This law of hidnat is consonant with the Quranic command as hereunder reminding mankind the pains and pangs which a mother has to bear for the evolution of the embryo within herself :

"And We have enjoined on man to be good to his parents; in travail upon travail did his mother bear him, in years twain was his weaning." (31st Sura Luqman, Verse 14).

"We have enjoined on man kindness to his parents: in pain did his mother bear him, and in pain did she give him birth." (46th Sura Ahqaf, verse 15).

<u>7. Thus, the Islamic law of hidnat is that the mother has absolute right against the father over the minor child till she remarries. It is to be noticed that the hadith quoted above does not specifically state that the right of hidnat will cease if she remarries. The hadith indicates that the right of hidnat of the mother then will be at par with that of the father and the case of the mother versus the father is to be decided vis-a-vis the minor's welfare.</u>

<u>8. Jurists of the schools of Sunnis and Shias had fixed different ages of the minor at which a mother loses her right of hidnat. We do not find any basis thereof either from the Quran or hadith. The opinions of the jurists arc, therefore, their respective personal opinions based on the social norms and conditions prevailing in their times and, as such, have no binding force.</u>

9. In the case of Hefzur Rahman vs. Shamsun Nahar reported in 47 DLR 54, I have observed as hereunder:

"That a civil Court has the jurisdiction to follow the law as in the Quran disregarding any other law on the subject, if contrary thereto even though laid down by the earlier jurists or commentators may be of great antiquity and high authority and though followed for a considerable period. Under the Hindu Law clear proof of usage can outweigh the written texts of law. But it is not in the case of Islamic law. For it is an article of faith of a Muslim that he should follow without questioning what has been revealed in Quran and disobedience thereof is a sin.

"Issue No. 2.

Admittedly on 21-12-95 the plaintiff voluntarily handed over the custody of the minors to the first defendant on the basis of a deed of agreement, the terms whereof in English are expressed as hereunder:

1. Second party Fakir Ashrafuddin Ahmed has paid an amount of Taka 1, 50,000.00 being the entire dues of the first party, Rumana Afrin, including her dower money for the dissolution of the marriage.

2. First party has handed over the custody of the minor daughters to the second party unconditionally and forever. 3. First party shall withdraw her criminal case and any other case, if filed, against the second party and in future she shall not file any case or shall not demand anything against the second party."

10. Mr. Chowdhury submits that the terms of the agreement debar the plaintiff to claim the custody of the daughters. Ms. Salma Masud Chowdhury, plaintiffs learned Advocate, in reply submits that the term No. 2 is without any consideration and was not voluntarily agreed upon.

11. Looking at the three terms as a whole, we find that the consideration of term No. 3 is the term No. 1, but term No. 2 is independent of the other two terms and is a promise. So the question is as to whether the plaintiff is estopped from claiming her legal right of hidnat for this promise.

12. Lord Denning in his book The Discipline of Law has defined promissory estoppel in the following language:

"It is a principle of justice and of equity. It comes to this: When a man, by his words or conduct, has led another to believe that he may safely act on the faith of them and the other does act on them he will not be allowed to go back on what he has said or done when it would be unjust or inequitable for him to do so."

13. We consider it absurd to apply this rule in the instant case. The answer to issue No. 2 is, therefore, no.

Issue No. 3.

Mr. Chowdhury argues at length pointing to the poverty of the plaintiff and her father that they are unable to up bring the minors in the same standard of living to which they have become accustomed. Under the law it is the father who has to maintain his minor child, be the child in his custody or in the custody of the mother. The argument of Mr. Chowdhury, therefore, fails and the issue No. 3 is decided in favour of the plaintiff.

Hence

Ordered

That the suit be and is decreed without costs against the defendants. Plaintiff is declared as the guardian and custodian of her minor daughters till she remarries.

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 22.7.80 passed by the High Court Division in Application No. 6 of 1976.
full_judgment:
Chowdhury A. T. M. Masud. J.-These two appeals by special leave arises from the judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division passed on July 22, 1980, in Application No. 6 of 1976 under section 66 (1) of the Income Tax Act. The Commissioner of Taxes Chittagong Zone is the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 114 of 1981, wherein leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division correctly interpreted provisions of sub-section 2(A) of section 34 of the Income Tax Act. The assesse is the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 115 of 1981 wherein leave was granted to consider whether the expression 'person' mentioned in sub-section (5) of section 5 of the Income Tax. Act was correctly interpreted by the High Court Division.

2. The assesse M/S. M. Ismail & Sons, which is a wholesale dealer in Yarn and Textile and Clearing and Forwarding Agent, was originally assessed income tax on 22nd July, 1950, on a total income of Tk. 44,702/-. On February 16, 1962, notice under section 34 of the Income Tax Act was issued upon it for re-assessment, the ground being that it was under-assessed for the year concerned. The assesse appeared and submitted return under protest and showed the income at Tk. 44,702/- the income which was originally shown claiming that no part of its income was under assessed or escaped assessment Thereupon notices under section 23(2) and 22(4) of the Income Tax Act were issued upon it, for the production of Books of Accounts and necessary evidence. The assesse, against whom the allegation was that it was imported cotton yarn of a total invoice value of Tk. 21,49,843/- which was not shown in its return, appeared and submitted its inability to produce the Books of Accounts and other documents as those could not be traced out due to lapse of time.

3. The Income Tax Officer then assessed tax summarily under section 23(4) of the Income Tax Act. Being aggrieved, the assesse preferred appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, who set aside the assess mention the ground that the .Income Tax Officer had not given any reason for summary assessment and directed the Income Tax Officer to made fresh assessment in accordance with law. On the points of jurisdiction and 'limitation, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that initiation of proceedings u/s 34 of the Act was valid and not barred by limitation. The assesse preferred a second appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. which allowed the appeal and annulled the order of re-assessment on the findings that (i) prior to 1963, the definition of 'person' did not include 'firm'; (ii) that the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to issue a fresh notice under section 34 of the income Tax Act and re-open the assessment.

4. Against the aforesaid order of the Appellate Tribunal. the Revenue filed Application No.6 of 1976 under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act before the High Court Division submitting, inter alia, the following questions of law which arose out of the order of the Tribunal; (1) whether the proceedings started by the Income Tax Officer under section 34 of the Income Tax Act was barred by limitation; (2) whether the word 'person' includes 'firm' of the assesse.

5. A Division Bench of the High Court Division answered the questions in the affirmative and held that (1) the issuance of notice upon the assesse for re-assessment under the amended provisions of section 34 was not in accordance with law as it existed at the relevant time and (2) that the expression 'person' as occurs in section 5(5) of the Income Tax Act does not exclude a 'firm' from its ambit.

6. In Civil Appeal No. 114 of 1981, the only point for determination is whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division correctly interpreted sub-section 2(A) of section 34 of the Income Tax Act.

7. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in the said appeal, contended that the High Court Division wrongly interpreted sub- section (2A) which clearly empowered the Income Tax Officer to issue a notice under section 34 (1) at any time, notwithstanding at the time of issue of such notice the period of 8 years specified in the said sub- section before its amendment had expired. He submits that the learned Judges of the High Court Division arrived at an erroneous conclusion as they failed to consider all the relevant provisions of law which would indicate that sub-section (2A) had retrospective effect. Mr. Bhuiyan argues that even if the 8 years' period mentioned in unamented provision of section 34(1) has expired, under section (2A), the Income Tax Officer was competent to issue fresh notice and reopen the assessment.

8 Mr. S. M. Hussain, the learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents in the said Civil Appeal No. 114 of 1981 argues that the High Court Division has correctly interpreted sub- section (2a) of Section 34 of the Income Tax Act. He contends that sub section (2A) came into force with effect from the 1st day of April, 1959 and it had no retrospective operation, so as to cover any assessment already barred by limitation, before the amendment came into force. Mr. Hussain submits that the impugned notice was issued on 16-2-62 and the original assessment was made on 7-7-50 The period of 8 years mentioned in the unamended provision of section 34(1) in the case of the assesse, expired on 31-3-59 and as such the Income Tax Officer was not competent to issue any fresh notice upon the assesse under the amended provision of section 34(1).

9. Admittedly, during assessment year 1950-51, relevant provision of law empowered the Income Tax Officer to issue a notice for re-assessment, if any income had escaped assessment of income tax at any time within 8 years prior thereto. By an amendment of section 34(1) of the Income Tax Act effective from 1st April, 1959, the provision of 8 years' limit was deleted and accordingly re-assessment could be made at any time. It is not disputed that a complete assessment may be re-opened, if the relevant provisions of law are amended with appropriate retrospective effect.

<u>10. Newly inserted sub-section (2A) of Section 34 which also came into effect from 1st April, 1959, provided that a notice under section 34(1) could still be issued at any time. It specifically provided that such notice could be issued notwithstanding that at the time of the issue of such notice, the period of 8 years as provided before the amendment of section 34(1) had already expired. Sub-section (2A) of Section 34 reads as follows:</u>

<u>"A notice under sub-section (1) may, where the Income Tax Officer has reason to believe that the assesse or any other person on his behalf has (***) concealed the particulars of his income or deliberately furnished inaccurate particulars thereof (***), be issued at any time notwithstanding that at the time of issue of such notice the period of eight years specified in the said sub-section before its amendment bad expired and no assessment or re-assessment made (or any other proceeding taken in consequence of any notice or any assessment or reassessment made under section 2(B) or any other proceeding taken in consequence of any notice issued for that purpose) shall be called in question in any Court, Tribunal or other authority merely on the ground that at the time the notice was issued or at the time the assessment or reassessment was made, the time within which such notice should have been made under this section as in force before its amendment had expired; provided that no notice under sub-section (1) shall be issued in respect of income, profits and gains, which were received or are deemed to have been received, or which accrued or arose or are deemed to have accrued or arisen to an assessed before the 14th day of August, 1947."</u>

<u>11. It may be noticed that in the said sub-section (2A), there is specific provision that no assessment or re-assessment made or any other proceeding taken in consequence of such notice shall be called in question in any Court, tribunal or other authority merely on the ground that at the time the notice was issued or at the time the assessment or re assessment was made the time within which such notice should have been issued or the assessment or the re-assessment should have been made under this section as in force before its amendment had expired. It appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division did not take into consideration all the material provisions of sub- section (2A) and as such it reached the erroneous conclusion that "when the amended provision of sub-section 2A of section 34 came into force on 1st April, 1959. 8 years from the assessment year, having already expired on 31st March, 1959 the Income Tax Officer could not issue any fresh notice upon the assesse under the amended provision of section 34 (1) of the Act on 16th February, 1962." The aforesaid observation of the learned Judges is clearly based on an erroneous interpretation of sub- section (2A). As observed earlier the sub-section has clearly provided for issuing such notice and reopening assessment, even after the period of 8 years had expired. The decisions cited by Mr. Hussain from Indian Courts are not of any assistance in this case, since some material provisions of sub-section (2A) are not to be found in the relevant sections of Indian Income Tax Act, which came into consideration by the Courts in the cited cases.</u>

<u>12. For the aforesaid reasons, the interpretation of sub-section (2A) of section 34 as given by the High Court Division cannot be said to lie correct. Accordingly, the impugned decision is set aside and Civil Appeal No. 114 of 1981 is allowed but without any order as to costs.</u>

13. In Civil Appeal 115 of 1981 the question for determination is whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division correctly interpreted the expression 'person' as contained in various provisions of the Income Tax Act. It is contended by Mr. Hussain the learned Counsel for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 115 of 1981 that the expression 'firm' was not included in the definition of 'person'. He argues that sub- section (5) of section 5 of the Act does not empower the Commissioner of Income Tax to confer jurisdiction on the assessing officer to perform his functions in respect of a firm because the sub- section contemplates assignment of cases 'person wise' or 'incomewise' coupled with an 'area'. He further argues that the expression 'firm' having own definition in the Act itself, no other definition could be attributed to it such as the expression 'person' includes a 'firm'.

14. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the respondent, contends that the High Court Division rightly held that the definition of 'person', made from time to time by various amendments of Income Tax Act, was always inclusive and not exclusive and that such definition of 'person' was never exhaustive to exclude a 'firm' simply because "firm" was included by subsequent amendment.

15. The learned Judges of the High Court Division observed that section 3 of the Income Tax Act, which is the charging section is comprehensive enough not only to include any partner of any firm or member of any association individually but also the firm and the association collectively. It was further observed that during the relevant assessment year 1950-51, the charging provision of section 3 of the Income Tax Act specifically included a firm.

<u>16. Sub-section (5) of section 5 should be read in conjunction with section 3 of the Income Tax Act and reading the two provisions together, it would be apparent that the relevant authority of the Income Tax Department was quite competent to assess incometax even upon a firm, because 'person' mentioned in sub-section (5) of section 5 included an association of persons or a firm or a company or a local authority as such.</u>

<u>Section 3 of the Income Tax Act which is the charging section provides that the Income Tax Officer may assess tax in respect of total income of previous year of every person.</u>

<u>17. Under clause (9) of section 2 'person includes an individual, Hindu undivided family, a firm, all association of persons or a body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, a Company, a local authority and every other artificial judicial person. Accordingly, 'firm' is a 'person' for the purpose of Income Tax Act and it is liable to be taxed for its total income for the previous year.</u>

<u>Section 3 provides that such person shall be charge at the specified rate in respect of the total income of the previous year if such firm becomes an assessed.</u>

<u>18. We are, therefore, of opinion that the learned Judges of the High Court Division correctly interpreted the expression 'person.'</u>

Accordingly, Civil Appeal No. 115 of 1981 is dismissed, without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J.- While concurring with the judgment just delivered by my learned brother I would like to add a few words of my own. Here is a case which has unfortunately been dealt with by the Administrator of Wakfs and the learned District Judge more on surmises and conjectures than with reference to the materials on record or to the law on the subject.

2. It appears that an application was filed by one Syed Amir Hossain before the Administrator of Wakfs for removal of the petitioner as Mutwalli of the Wakf estate. Curiously enough, the parties were not allowed to lead any evidence nor the allegations were allowed to be tested by any cross-examination nor the application for removal of the mutwalli was supported by any affidavit. This, in our opinion has cut at the very root of the entire proceeding. Upon what materials the Administrator of Wakfs based his decision to remove the petitioner as Mutwalli, is beyond our understanding.

3. The learned Advocate for the opposite party, Mr. Habibur Rahman has however taken a point as to limitation. It appears that the proceeding was started long back before the Administrator of Wakfs. After the decision of the Administrator removing the Mutwalli, an appeal was preferred before the District Judge which was also dismissed. As against that, a review application under order 47 rules 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed which however was dismissed for default. Thereafter, the petitioner Mrs. Nadira Rahman preferred Civil Revision No. 1429 of 1977 before this Court which was disposed of by the Court with the following order:-

"Heard the learned Advocates of both sides. The petitioner can get relief under Order 4-7 rule 7 sub-rule (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such the petitioner may take recourse to it. In this view of the matter the rule is disposed of"

The petitioner in accordance with the direction of this Court then filed an application under Order 47 rule 7(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned District Judge however rejected the same also as being barred by limitation. The petitioner thereafter moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. It will thus be seen that the petitioner has been prosecuting with due diligence the instant proceeding whether before a court of first instance or before a court of appeal or before a court of revision against the same party for the same relief which however, for want of jurisdiction, was unable to grant the desired relief. Furthermore, it is now well settled that the Limitation Act does not provide for any period of limitation for an application in revision. This has been clearly laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Muhammad Swaleh and another Vs. Messers United Grain &Fodder Agencies reported in 16 D.L R. (S.C) 15Sas follows :-

"The Limitation Act does not provide for any period of Limitation for application in revision. The only article which could be applicable was the residuary Article 181 which provides a limitation of three years for an application, but even that Article will not stand in the way of the exercise of revisional power for these powers can be exercised suo motu. At the same time it should be remembered that the respondents had themselves approached the High Court in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction and once the High Court is seized of the case in the exercise of such jurisdiction it cell in accordance with section 115, C.P.C. "make such order in the case as it thinks fit”

Having regard to these facts and circumstances and our discussion above, we find that there is no substance in the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the opposite party on the point of limitation. With regard to the other points raised, these have been stated and discussed in details by my learned brother in his judgment. But it should be pointed out that both the Administrator of Wakfs and the learned District Judge appeared to be unduly concerned about the factum of the petitioner's appointment as a Mutwalli which, in our opinion was no issue at all so far as the question of her removal was concerned. This appears to have unduly and unnecessarily influenced both of them and should and ought to have been avoided. Having regard to these facts and circumstances and our discussion above, I concur with my learned brother and make the Rule absolute. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we direct the parties to bear their own costs.

Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury J.- This Rule is directed against a judgment and order dated 25.5.72 passed by District Judge, Bakerganj passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 186 of 1974.

4. Facts in brief are that opposite party Sayed Amir Hossain, son of late Syed Mohammad Ahsan filed a petition against the petitioner Nadira Rahman before the Administrator of Wakf under section 32 of Wakf Ordinance No. 1 of 1962 for removing her from the mutwatiship of Saleha Khatun Wakf Estate, enrolled under E.C. Nos. 1510 and 1511-A on the allegation the said Nadira Rahman not· only was improperly appointed as Muwali of the said Estate on 29.7.64 by the Wakf Administrator but that she never had managed or looked after the Wakf Estate or had performed any of the functions imposed bythe Wakf deed, she had misappropriated Taka 2,000/- and also obtained the order of eviction against Sayed Amir Hossain by instituting a false case of trespass. The petitioner Nadira Rahman having learnt the allegation against her filed a written objection before the Administrator of Wakfs denying all the allegations as manifestly false and concocted slaiming that she was legally and properly appointed as Mutwalli of the said Estate by the Wakf Administrator on the written proposal submitted by her father Syed Mohammad Ahsan, the then Mutwalli and that her appointment had also been consented to by Syed Amir Hossain, the opposite party, who happen to be her brother, before the Mutwali and there was no case of any illegal appointment or exercise of power without any lawful authority and that she had always managed the wakf property according to the wishes of the Wakfs and there was no question of mismanagement or misappropriation of the wakf annuity or any fraud as alleged. The matter was heard by the Administrator of Wakfs and on the basis of this written reply and without any further reference by the Administrator of Wakfs to any other evidence he passed the order dated 1.11.74 allowing the application filed by Syed Mohammad Amir Hossain and ordered the petitioner before this court, Mrs. Nadira Rahman to be removed from mutwalli ship and finding the petitioner before the Administrator or Wakfs, namely Syed Mohammad Amir Hassain be a fit person to the next Mutwalli according to the terms of the wakf deed, appointed him as Mutwalli in place of Mrs. Nadira Rahman. She was directed to hand over the charge of mutwalli ship to Syed Mohammad Amir Hossain immediately. As against that order an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 186 of 1974 was filed before the District Judge, Bakerganj by Mrs. Nadira where it was alleged that the Administrator of Wakfs without applying his judicial mind and on the basis of no evidence, bad passed the illegal order removing the petitioner from mutwalliship by appointing her brother as mutwalli. The learned District Judge, after hearing the parties however dismissed the appeal on contest with cost and the order of the Administrator of Wakfs dated 1-11-74 was affirmed. As against the said judgment and order of the learned District Judge the petitioner had obtained this Rule from this Court.

5. We have heard Mr. Abdur Rhaman Biswas with Mr. Sk. Atiar Rahman, the learned Advocate in support of the Rule and Mr. Habibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing against it.

6. Mr. Abdur Rahman Biswas, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner having taken us through the judgment of the learned District Judge as well as that of the Administrator of Wakfs has contended that the learned District Judge, in exercise of his jurisdiction acted illegally and with material irregularity inasmuch as the learned District Judge had no legal evidence before him to confirm the order of the Administrator of Wakfs removing the petitioner from the office of the mutwalliship. He has further argued that the learned District Judge and the Administrator of Wakfs did not at all consider the position of law and the provisions of section 32(1) of the Waqfs Ordinance in removing the petitioner and as such the judgment and order are liable to be set aside.

7. The learned Advocate appearing against the Rule, on the other hand has contended that the learned District Judge passed the judgment and order dated 25.5.72 in removing the petitioner Nadira Rahman from mutwalli ship, and confirming the order of the Administrator of Wakfs dated 1.11.74 with jurisdiction and there was no question of any assumption of jurisdiction not vested in it by law and there was also no question of any illegal or material irregularity having been committed by the courts below in the exercise of their jurisdiction as vested under law. The rule therefore bearing no substance needs to be discharged and the impugned orders affirmed.

8. We have considered the argument advanced by both the parties and examined the records. This is an application under revisional jurisdiction of this court and we are conscious of the limitation of this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Under this section, an allegation that the courts below had not taken into consideration the relevant provisions of law, would not by itself attract the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure unless it can be shown further that there was such a violation of some statutory provision of law or the principles of natural justice as would render the proceedings coram-non-judice. In the instant case the whole thing started because of an application submitted by the opposite party namely Syed Amir Hossain for removal of the petitioner Nadira Rahman from Mutwalliship. The said application that was submitted before the Wakf Administrator was an application under section 32 of the Wakfs Ordinance, No.1 of 1962. Section 32 of the said Ordinance contains the necessary grounds and procedure for removal of a Mutwalli in certain cases, on certain specific allegations having been proved and be removed either by the Administrator himself on his own motion suo motu or on an application filed by any person. It further provided that the Mutwalli in order to be removed must be given an opportunity of being heard and reply to the allegations, if any made against him. All these had been spelt out and contained in the provisions under section 32 of the said Ordinance. The proviso to the said section provided that no such order of removal of a mutwalli could be made without giving him an opportunity of being heard. It is the cardinal principle of interpretation of any Deed or Statute that the proviso to a section is to be regarded to have an overriding effect and control over the whole section. This is a mandatory provision as to interpretation of law disregard of which would nullify all action taken under the said section.

9. Under section 32 of the Waqf Ordinance a Mutwalli may be removed for breach of trust, mismanagement, malfeasance or misappropriation. He can also be removed for any act causing loss of the wakf property or affecting the proper administration, control or preservation of the wakf and also when he had been convicted under section 61 of this Ordinance and lastly, if he is found unsuitable, incompetent, negligent or otherwise undesirable. The Wakf Administrator, therefore, in removing the Mutwalli, has a duty under the law to be satisfied that the allegations made against the Mutwalli come within the mischief of section 32 of the Ordinance and that the Mutwalli had been given a reasonable opportunity of controverting the allegations as made against him. Thus, out of necessity the Administrator of Wakfs had to confine himself within the facts which would come within the mischief of law as has been spelt out in section 32 of the Ordinance itself. Any other irrelevant statement of fact and its irrelevant consideration not within the mischief of section 32 would be an illegality. If any other fact is considered by the Administrator of Wakfs in removing the Mutwalli from his port of Mutwalli ship not coming within the mischief of section 32 it would be an exercise of power beyond the power and therefore, illegal and without jurisdiction making the whole proceeding coram non judice.

10. Sub-clause (1) of sub- sec. (1) of sec. 32 of the Ordinance speaks or a breach of trust and also of mismanagement, malfeasance and misappropriation. The very definition of the offences speak of mental condition, something of a guilty mind on the part of the Mutwalli in mismanaging the trust in violation of the condition of trust thereby causing a loss of Wakf property, or misappropriating trust fund. An these words are of the same agnatic group which speaks of a guilty mind and results of deeds and misdeeds but not the result of inaction. The second groups of words are the results of inaction rather than of action and they thus belong to another group of words of the some genus distinct from the first group. In the group the word 'Unsuitable' in sub-clause (4) under sub-section (1) of section 32 is followed by the words incompetent, negligent or otherwise undesirable'. These second group of words speaks of incapacity of a person to work as a Mutwalli. All these are questions of fact which need detailed investigation and need be proved strictly within the framework of a strict definition of the words found in section 32 of the ordinance to the satisfaction of the Administrator of Wakes on .evidence on record. Further, section 32 of the Waqfs Ordinance is something of a penal statute which punishes the Mutwalli by taking away the vested right of a Mutwalli to continue as a Mutwalli which right is something of a proprietary right, and is liable to be vested in a person unless taken away in due course of law. Because of this sense of penalty the law givers in their anxiety had made it incumbent upon the Administrator of Wakfs to hear the person who is an accused before him and him hear before he is penalised and before he is found guilty of the allegations made. The Administrator of Wakfs being a court of law while acting under section 32 of the Ordinance need to come to a finding as a court of law. Hence, if the finding arrived at was based on no evidence at all or on irrelevant facts and without following the procedure it would be an illegal finding and it would amount to an exercise of power with material irregularity making a proceeding coram non judice.

11. Keeping this legal position in view let us now consider how far the natural justice clause that had been incorporated by the proviso to section 32 of the Wakf Ordinance No. 1 of 1962 had been complied With before the penalty was imposed. On a reference to the records it is seen that except the written objection submitted by the Petitioner Nadira Rahman before the Wakf Administrator she had not been given any opportunity of adducing any further evidence before the Wakf Administrator in defence nor the petitioner before the Wakf Administrator, who happened to be brother of Mrs. Nadira Rahman adduced any evidence in support of his allegation as contained in his petition which however need to have been proved as an allegation contained in a plaint in a court of law. Thus, it is clearly seen that the Administrator of Wakfs without following the mandatory provision of law as to hearing as provided under the proviso to section 32 of Wakf Ordinance came to a finding as to the incapacity and unworthiness of the Mutwalli Mrs. Nadira Rahman on the basis of no evidence on record and without giving the petitioner an opportunity of been heard and without asking the complainant to prove his own allegations by examining witness, which is the minimum requirement of law. This ought to have been done because the proceeding before the Wakf Administrator was not a mere administrative or domestic proceeding. The Wakf Administrator is to function as a court of law following all the norms and procedure of a court as if dealing with litigants before a court. Even the domestic tribunals which are not guided by any statutory rules are required to follow the rules of natural justice as spelt out by Superior Courts and it was held that a person can never be penalised unless he is given a due hearing even by the domestic tribunals. It is not merely a procedural matter as to hearing. It is a substantive right of being heard.

12. On a reference to the order of the Administrator of Wakfs and also to the judgment of the learned District Judge it appears that certain extraneous facts had really played a prominent part in forming their opinion as to the alleged undesirability and incapacity of the petitioner Nadira Rahman in discharging her duties of a Mutwalli, and that was that Nadira Rahman allegedly somehow managed to get herself appointed as a Matwalli by the Administrator of Wakfs upon a recommendation submitted by her father when he was ill and that was the result of undue influence She was an absentee Mutwalli and thus incapable of acting properly as such. That was also considered to be a factor by the learned District Judge in affirming the order of the Wakf Administrator. It was on these grounds only that the courts found her incapable of managing the Wakf estate since her appointment in 1964 and was removed from the post of a mutwalli in the better interest of the wakf estate. The learned District Judge found that the father of Nadira Rahman, who was the previous Mutwalli of the estate, first filed an application before the Wakf Administrator nominating his first son Syed Mohammad Nizamuddin as his successor Mutwalli and his second son succeeding the first son as Mutwalli but the said matter was kept on record with the observation that the issue would be considered when the question of succession of Mutwalli arose after the death of the father of Nadira Rahman. Subsequently, however, the father of Nadira Rahman resigned on, 23.9.64 on health grounds with a new proposal for Nadira Rahman as the next Mutwalli. It was found by the court that during his illness he lived under care of his dauhter Mrs. Nadira Rahman and his son-in-law Fazlur Rahman at Karachi and that he was taken to Karachifor treatment by Mrs. Nadira Rahman.

13. The court found that this fact suggests that the MutwaIli was prevailed upon by the petitioner Nadira Rahman or her husband Fazlur Rahman to modify the original proposal and to nominate her instead of her brother, at next Mutwalli. It had further been found by the court that Mrs. Nadira Rahman was an absentee mutwalli and although her term of office as mutwalli she managed the wakf estate only through her husband and after his death she became a helpless widow and thus not at all competent to manage the wakf property, These conclusions as to obtaining original Mutwalli by undue influence and her subsequent incapacity as a mutwalli because of her absence from Barisal was arrived at by a curious process of reasoning which is not understood by us. A daughter looking after her father would not look after her father at his old age out of any malafide design. That would not be the general ordinary conduct of a daughter or for that matter of any children as being foreign to human nature if not proved to be otherwise being an exception in a given case of which normal human conduct or behaviour acting in good faith would be taken notice of by a court under section 114 of the Evidence Act. Nadira Begum's father was not under the Patria protesta of Nadira Begum nor his position was that of a Pardhnashin Lady having no independent advice or of a minor where the law may presume the existence of undue influenced and hence if her father was unduly influenced in suggesting her name the said design ought to have been made a specific Issue and proved after evidence led being an exception to general human conduct without which the inference drawn as to undue influence would be based on no evidence at all but on mere surmises and conjectures by shifting the burden on the wrong party.It was the petitioner who was claiming undue influence so it was for him to prove that.

14. There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction. Hence, he who pleads bad faith need to prove the same. Here comes the wrong burden of proof. And in this case the petitioner had not discharged that burden as to undue influence. Further, the fact that Nadera Begum was not living in the place where the property was situated would not warrant a conclusion that she being an absentee, Mutwalli would be incompetent or unsuitable as a mutwalli. The allegation of mismanagement or incompetency, if any need to have been proved by evidence and the said cannot be proved solely on the allegation of being a non-resident at the place where the property was situated because the law does not at all contemplate any such absence as a disqualification under section 32 of the Ordinance.

15. Words indicating a genus and consequential species in a Statute are not only deemed to be followed by similar words of the same genus by following the ejusdem generals rules but also that the meaning of the more general words would always be restricted to a sense more analogous to that of the Jess general words by following the rule guided by the maxim Nocitur a sociis Thus, the words incompetent, negligent or otherwise undesirable as in section 32 of the Ordinance would only include acts arising out of negligence or acts analogous to that of negligence being the less, general word used in the section and they would not include "absentee" being not of the same genus or of the same agnatic group and also being not analogous to the Jess general word in that group nor the word "otherwise undesirable" would include any word of a different genus then the proceeding words but restricted to less general word namely negligence in that section. Hence, to induct the word absentee in section 32 of the Ordinance would amount to legislation by the Imposition of a disqualification to which a Mutwalli was never subjected to under the scheme of the Act. Again to include absence as a disqualification by interpretation would lead to absurdity and impossibility of performance as the Wakf property may be situated at different places of the country and a Mutwalli cannot physically be resident at all the places at the same time. This impossibility cannot be the intention of the legislature. It would also bring in the illegal presumption that a person would not or could not manage his property nor manage his property through his Agents. Of course in a given case the law may impose such a restriction relating to a particular property for Iimited period of for some time but in its absence a court of law cannot read in to the law such restriction which is not there by implication.

16. Statutes imposing penalties or which take away right must be strictly construed. A court of law must always see that the person to be penalised comes fairly and squarely within the plain words of the enactment. It is not enough that what he done or not done comes substantially within the mischief of the law otherwise the wide discretion that would be claimed by the courts in interpreting laws to fit in a given fact would give rise to a question of Chancellors foot and in the language of Lord Tomlin, J. as observed in L.R.C. Vs. Duke of Westminster. reported in 36 A. C. at page 1 "the sooner this misunderstanding is dispelled and the supposed doctrine given its quietus the better it will be for all concerned for the doctrine seems to involve substituting the uncertain and crooked cord of discretion for the golden and straight met word of Law".

17. The learned Judge affirmed the order of the Administrator of Wakfs without taking into consideration these legal aspects of the matter. When a court takes into consideration irrelevant matters when relevant matters are omitted from consideration when the court omitted to consider the way to be followed are mandatory to be followed as a procedure by a court of law the court acts in a manner causing material irregularity rendering the proceeding non-existent in the eye of law because then would come the question of jurisdiction and an illegal exercise of the same when it never existed which is not a question of passing a wrong order or a right one with jurisdiction. In the instant case the non-observance of the principle of natural justice clause, the observance of which only would confer upon the Administrator the jurisdiction and the power to initiate a proceeding leading to the removal of the mutwalli and consideration of irrelevant facts not with mischief of the Act would render the proceeding a nullity and that would confer upon this court the power to interfere under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in its Revisional Jurisdiction.

18. A last point was taken to the effect that this Revisional application itself is not maintainable as it was filed beyond time. We find no substance in that contention also as it is seen from record that the petitioner on wrong surmise applied before the wrong forum one after the other. This will save limitation under of the provision of the Limitation Act. No other points urged.

19. We thus find that non observance of the principle of natural justice and failure to act as a court of law and consideration of irrelevant matters in arriving at a finding of fact not within the mischief of section 32 had rendered the proceeding before the Administrator of Wakrs a nullity. The judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, affirming those of the Administrator of Wakfs is therefore, liable to be set aside and also that of the Administrator of Wakfs in removing the petitioner mutwalli.

20. In the result this rule is made absolute. The judgment and order of the learned District Judge affirming those passed by the Administrator of Wakfs in removing the petitioner Mutwalli is hereby set aside, being illegal. The petitioner Nadera Begum is directed to be appointed as Mutwalli as she was before the impugned orders were passed and she is to continue as mutwalli till she resigns or is removed in accordance with law.

No order as to cost.

End.

parties:
The Azad & Publications Ltd & others
Vs.
Md. Quamrul Anam Khan & another
full_judgment:
FAZLE MUNIM J.:- This appeal arises from the judgment and order of a Bench of the High Court Division passed in Appeal No. 4 of 1970 on July 24, 1975 affirming the judgment and order of the company Judge of the Dacca High Court passed in Company matter No. 41 of 1969 on August 27, 1970.

2. The respondent No. 1 Md. Quamrul Anam Khan filed an application under section 38 of the Companies Act for rectification of the Share Register of The Azad and Publications Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Company). This company was registered on April 10, 1960 with authorised capital of Rs. 10,00,000/- divided into 10 thousand shares 100 rupees each. The company was incorporated with four permanent Directors, namely, (1) Late Md. Sadrul Anam Khan, (2) Md. Badrul Anam Khan, (3) Md. Quamrul Anam Khan, (4) Late Moulana Md. Akram Khan. Moulana Md. Akram Khan and Md. Quamrul Anam were elected Chairman of the Board of Directors and Managing Director of the Company respectively. The term of office of Md. Quamrul Anam Khan was extended from time to time and he was reelected as the Managing Director in the Annual General Meeting of the Company held on December 26, 1966 for a period of 3 years. On the death of Sadrul Anam Khan, Md. Zainul Anam Khan was appointed temporary Director. This term of his as Director expired on December 31, 1968. On the death of Moulana Md. Akram Khan on August 18, 1968. Badrul Anam Khan was elected Chairman on December, 4, 1968. On December 6, 1968 the Chairman convened Annual General Meeting on December 31, 1968. The meeting was not, however, held on this date. A criminal case was started as a result of which respondent No. 1 was arrested. Appellant No. 2 took possession of the office premises of the company on February 2, 1969 styling himself as the Managing Director. A special resolution passed in Extra-Ordinary General Meeting of the shareholders. Appellant No. 4 was appointed as permanent Director of the Company in the vacancy caused by the death of Moulana Akram Khan. He was authorised to act temporarily as Chairman of the Company in place of respondent No. 2. Appellant No. 3 was elected as the Director of the Company. Appellant No. 2 filed a return of allotment of shares in the name of certain person. No notice was served on respondent No. 1 and other shareholders of the Company.

3. The case of the appellants was that the appellant No. 2 was appointed Managing Director in the Annual General Meeting held on December 31, 1968 for a period of one year and in the Ninth Annual General Meeting held on November 23, 1969 he was appointed permanent Director on the death of his father Md. Sadrul Anam Khan. Md. Quamrul Anam Khan was not elected the Managing Director of the Company. Respondent No. 2 Badrul Anam Khan was Chairman prior to July 15, 1969 and Mrs. Salem Khanam, wife of Md. Sadrul Anam Khan was elected Chairman in the Extra-Ordinary General Meeting held on July 15, 1969. There was violence and death in the family as a result of which arrests were made by the Police. It was claimed by the appellants that all the meetings namely, the General meetings of the share holders and the Board meetings were duly held after service of notices and, therefore, actions done in pursuance of the meetings were valid and binding.

4. By his judgment and order dated 27.8.70 the Company Judge allowed the application and gave direction to rectify the share register of the Company by deleting 630 shares in question allotted to the appellants. As regards service of notice under certificate of posting the learned Company Judge held that the presumption of service being not available in the absence of registered service and the appellants having failed to prove due service of notice upon the respondents, their plea of proper service of notice could not be acceptable. Against this order the appellants preferred an appeal, Company Appeal No. 4 of 1970, which was dismissed with costs. The learned Judges of the High Court Division observed as follows:

"It is true that the Article does not require that notice is to be sent by registered post, but in order to avail of the benefits of the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act, ordinary service under certificate of posting is not sufficient unless notice is sent by registered post, the statutory presumption is not available''.

5. Being aggrieved, the appellants moved this court and obtained leave to appeal on the following two grounds:-

I. Because in view of the provision in the Article of Association of the Company prescribing the mode of service of notice regulations 49 and 112 of the Companies Act, the learned Judges of the High Court Division are not justified in holding with reference to section 27 of the General Clauses Act that notice is to be sent by registered post so as to avail of statutory presumption as to service and that ordinary service under certificate of posting is not sufficient.

II. Because the court of appeal below failed to consider that it is not "actual service which is the requirement of law but a honafide attempt to cause service at the addresses of the persons concerned, registered in the office of the Company."

6. Mr. "Khondker Mahhubuddin Ahmed, counsel for the appellant’s, submitted that in view of the provisions of the Articles of Association of the Company which are based on the provisions of the Companies Act and the liptigned notices having been served accordion such provisions, the learned Judges were wrong in holding that the presumptions of section 114 of the Evidence Act was not available since the impugned notices were not sent by registered post, certificate of posting being not sufficient to raise the presumption under the aforesaid section.

7. The controversy between the parties in this appeal arose over the allotment of shares of the company in the names of persons mentioned below."

Mrs. Salima Khatun 		50

Mrs. Fatema Hasan 		20

Md. Zainul Anam Khan 	130

Md. Shafiul Anam Khan 	130

Mrs. Rabeya Khanam 		20

Md. Shahedul Anam Khan 	130

Miss Rokeya Khanam 	20

Master Shahidul Anam Khan 130

Total 630

8. The allotment is said to have been by the appellant No. 2 on July 28, 1969. The respondent No. 1 asserted that the notice of meeting in which the allotment was alleged to have been made was not served upon him. He also denied that no Extra-Ordinary Meeting of the share-holders was ever held on July 15, 1969. According to him, the allotments referred to above were not legal and as such not binding upon the shareholders Respondent No. 1, therefore, prayed for rectification of the share register.

9. The provisions for rectification of the Share Register of the Company are contained in section 38 of the Companies Act which reads as follows:-

38.--(1) If—

(a) the name of any person is fraudulently or without sufficient cause entered in or omitted from the register of members of a company ; or

(b) default is made or unnecessary delay takes place in entering on the register the fact of any person having ceased to be a member, the person aggrieved, or any member of the company, or the company, may apply to the court for rectification of the register.

(2) The court may either refuse the application, or may order rectification of the register and payment by the company of any damages sustained by any party aggrieved, and may make such order as to costs as it in its discretion thinks fit.

(3) On any application under this section the Court may decide any question relating to the title of any person who is a party to the application to have his name entered in or omitted from the register, whether the question arises between members or alleged members, or between members or alleged members on the one hand and the company on the other hand; and generally may decide any question necessary or expedient to be decided for rectification of the register:

Provided that the court may direct an issue to be tried in which any question of law may be raised; and an appeal from the decision on such an issue shall lie in the manner directed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, on the grounds mentioned in section 100 of that Code.

10. This section empowers the court to decide the question raised in the present case as to whether the names of certain persons entered in the Share Register of the Company have been validly entered. This would depend on the valid allotment of shares to appellants Nos. 2-9 by the resolution of the Board of Directors alleged to have been passed on July 20, 1965. Notices of the Meeting of the Board on July 20, 1965 were claimed to have been sent to the share holders under certificate of posting. This according to the appellants, was proper service as required under the provisions of the Articles of Association of the Company and Regulation 112 of Table-A of the First Schedule of the Companies Act. Article 114 of the Articles of Association provides as follows:

114. Notice may be given to the members in the manner provided by Regulation 49 of the table by serving it personally or by sending it by post or by advertisement in a daily newspaper circulating in the district where the registered office of the company is situated."

Regulation 112 and not Regulation 49 of Table-A which provides the manner of service of notice is as follows:-

112.(1) A notice may be given by the company to any member either personally or by sending it by-post to him to his registered address or if he has no registered address in Bangladesh to the address, if any, Within Bangladesh supplied by him to the company for the giving of notices to him.

(2) Where a notice is sent by post, service of the notice shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, prepaying and posting a letter containing the notice and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post.

11. It was emphatically asserted by the appellants learned counsel that this being proper service, the notices must be accepted to have been served on the share holders even though they were not sent by registered post. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that the presumption of service was available in case of service of notice under certificate of posting as well.

12. According to the learned Judges of the High Court Division service of notice under certificate of posting does not raise the presumption under section 114 of Evidence Act. In order to avail of the presumption under the aforesaid section notice has to be sent by registered post, service under certificate of posting being not sufficient Mr. Nurullah, counsel for the respondents, asserted that in view of the provisions of section 27 of the General Clauses Act which were also taken into consideration by the learned Judges of the High Court Division the presumption claimed by the appellants was not available. Section 27 of the General Clauses Act reads as follows:

"Meaning of service by post—Where any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorises or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expressions "serve" or either of the expressions "Give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, prepaying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post."

<u>13. Reading the relevant provisions of the Articles of Association of the Company and Regulation 112 as well as section 27 of the general Clauses Act, it appears that when a notice is claimed to have been served by post, the presumption of service of such notice will be raised if the notice was sent by registered post. Such presumption is, however, neither conclusive nor irrefutable. In other words, the person to whom the letter or notice is addressed is at liberty to prove that it was not in fact served upon, nor received by him. Even though no presumption arises in case of a letter sent under certificate of posting, the respondents have been found to have proved that no such notices were even received by them. Excepting the claim that the notices of the impugned Board meeting were sent to the respondents under certificate of posting, the appellants have not succeeded in meeting the challenge of the respondents that they were never received by them by producing evidence to that effect. We, therefore, find no reason to differ from the views expressed by the learned Judges of the High Court Division regarding non-availability of the Statutory presumption of service, and this being so the conclusions raised by them must be upheld.</u>

The appeal is accordingly dismissed with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Delwar Hossain, J:-  This Rule Nisi was issued upon an application under Article 1 02(2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondent No. 1 to show cause as to why the respondent No. 1 shall not be directed to issue the certified copies of the Returns already submitted by the petitioner in the office of the respondent No.1 and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The petitioner filed the writ petition stating that the petitioner is a Public Limited Company by Shares incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 and obtained license under Section 4 (1) of the Financial Institutions Act, 1993 on 3.72010 and since then has been carrying its business as per its Memorandum of Association. The petitioner has been regularly filing Returns in the prescribed format of the respondent No. 1 namely Form XII, Schedule X and Form XV. The Bangladesh Bank by Circular No. DFIM Circular No. 09 dated 4.11.2009 directed all the Financial Institutions to increase their paid-up capital to Tk. 50 Crores through Initial Public Offering (IPO). In order to go for IPO it is mandatory to submit copies of all the Returns certified by the respondent No.1 for which the petitioner on several occasions requested the respondent No.1 to supply the certified copies of the Returns to be submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) but the respondent No.1 did not provide with the certified copies of the Returns without assigning any reason. Upon repeated request the office of the respondent No. 1 by letter No.RYSC-3096 dated 10,1.2008 informed the petitioner that as the file of the petitioner is under investigation by the Anti-Corruption Commissions, certified copies of the Returns cannot be provided. Thereafter the petitioner by its letter dated 23.3.2009 annexing the letter dated 10.1.2008 requested the Anti-Corruption Commission to instruct the respondent No.1 to issue the certified copies of the Returns filed by the petitioner. The respondent No.2, Anti-corruption Commission by its letter dated 13.4.2009 informed the respondent No. 1 that the petitioner may be provided with the certified copies of the Returns. Inspite of that the respondent No.1 refrained from issuing the certified copies of all the Returns submitted by it nor gave any reasons for not supplying the same. Finding no other alternative serving demand justice notice upon the respondent No.1 with a request to supply the certified copies of the Returns, tiled this writ petition. 

3. The respondent No.1 did not contest the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition. 

4. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that under section 347 of the Companies Act, 1994 any person has the right to obtain certified copies of the Returns on payment of prescribed fees. The respondent No. 1 is bound to supply the certified copies of the Returns submitted by the petitioner. The respondent No.1 in violation of section 347 of the Act, 1994 illegally refrained from supplying the certified copies of the Returns inspite of several request of the petitioner. The respondent No. 1 inspite of the letter dated 13.4.2009 issued by the respondent No. 2, Anti-corruption Commission refrained from issuing the certified copies of the Returns submitted by the petitioner. He thus submits that the respondent No.1 is liable to be directed to issue the certified copies of the Returns submitted by the petitioner by making the Rule absolute. 

5. No one appears on behalf of the respondent No.1 to oppose the Rule. 

6. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and perused the writ petition along with the annexures. 

7. It appears that the petitioner, a Financial Institution incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 and obtaining license under section 4(1) of the Financial Institutions Act, 1993 has been carrying its business as per its Memorandum of Association. The petitioner in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 has been regularly submitting its Returns in Form XII, Schedule X and Form XV. The petitioner is entitled to get the certified copies of the Returns on payment of prescribed fees as provided in Section 347 of the Companies Act, 1994 and the respondent No.1 is legally bound to provide the certified copies of the Returns on demand. But it appears that the respondent No. 1 refrained from issuing the certified copies of the Returns to the petitioner inspite of several request. 

8. It further appears that the respondent No.1 by a letter dated 10.1.2008 (Annexure-C) informed the petitioner that as the file of the petitioner was under investigation by the Anti-Corruption Commission, certified copies of the Returns could not be supplied. From the letter dated 13.4.2009 (Annexure-G) it appears that Anti-Corruption only seized the shares in the petitioner company only in respect Mr. M.A.H. Selim and his son Mr. Mahedi Hasan and other than these two shareholders other shareholders were not involved in connection with Ramna Police Station Case No.29 dated 6.12.2007 and accordingly requested the respondent No.1 to take necessary steps to issue certified copies of the Returns. Inspire of that the respondent No. 1 refrained from issuing the certified copies of the Returns to the petitioner. 

9. In the facts and circumstances of the case the respondent No.1 is liable to be directed to provide the petitioner with the certified copies of the Returns submitted by it. 
10. For the reasons discussed above the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. 

11. The respondent No.1, the Registrar of the Joint Stock Companies and Firms is hereby directed to issue the certified copies of the Returns already submitted by the petitioner within 2(two) weeks from the date of receipt of this judgment and order. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Quddus, J: These two writ petitions between the same parties involving common questions of facts and law have been heard together and are being disposed of by one judgment.

In writ petition 8173 of 2010 the Rule was issued challenging the proceedings in Artha Jari Case No.165 of 2004 (arising out of Title Suit No.10 of 1998), while in writ petition 8174 of 2010 the proceedings in Artha Jari Case No.114 of 2004 (arising out of Title Suit No.9 of 1998) was challenged. Both the execution cases are now pending before the Artha Rin Adalat consisting of the Joint District Judge, First Court, Barisal Facts leading to issuance of the Rules as it appears from the record, in brief, are that respondent 2 Janata Bank Ltd. instituted two suits, namely, Title Suit No.9 of 1998 for realization of loan amounting to Taka 42,00,356/= and Title Suit No.10 of 1998 for realization of Taka 23,31,315/= before the Artha Rin Adalat and Subordinate Judge, Barisal. In both the suits the writ petitioner as borrower and one Abdul Mannan Khan as guarantor were made defendants 1 and 2 respectively. Ultimately Title Suit No.9 of 1998 was decreed exparte in preliminary form on 29.07.1998 and Title Suit No.10 of 1998 was decreed on 28.07.1998 in the same manner. On two separate applications filed by the plaintiff-bank final decrees were passed on 31.08.1998 in both the suits. Thereafter, the decree holder-bank put the decrees in execution by filling Title Execution Case Nos.30 and 31 of 1998 before the Artha Rin Adalat consisting of the Subordinate Judge, Barisal. Subsequently the said execution cases were transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat consisting of the Joint District Judge, First Court, Barisal and were renumbered as Artha Jari Case Nos.114 and 165 of 2004 respectively. On separate applications filed by the decree holder-bank, the executing Court issued warrants of arrest against the petitioner by orders dated 24.01.2004 and 28.04.2004 respectively. Those warrants were pending for execution in which stage the decree holder-bank filed applications for issuance of certificates under section 33 (5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter called the Act, 2003), which were allowed the accordingly certificates under the said section were issued. Thereafter, the decree holder-bank filed two other applications for issuance of certificates under section 33 (7) of the Act, 2003, which the executing Court allowed by orders dated 12.03.2006 in both the execution cases. After more than four and half years from issuing the certificates, the petitioner moved in this Court with these writ petitions and obtained the Rules.

Respondent 2 Janata Bank Ltd. contests the Rules by filing two sets of affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits thereto contending, inter alia, that the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Barisal rightly proceeded with the execution cases and there is nothing wrong to interfere.

Mr. Shamim Khaled Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the Joint District Judge, First Court, Barisal was a civil court and not vested with the jurisdiction of Artha Rin Adalat and as such it proceeded illegally with the Artha Jari Case No.114 of 2004 from 19.05.2004 and with Artha Jari Case No.165 of 2004 from 20.05.2004.

In second fold of argument Mr. Khaled submits that the executing Court after issuance of certificates under section 37 (5) of the Act, 2003 disposed of Artha Jari Case No.114 of 2004 by order dated 17.03.2005 and disposed of Artha Jari Case No.165 of 2004 by order dated 30.03.2005 and became functus officio. Thereafter, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to proceed further with the execution cases and issue the certificates under section 33 (7) of the Act, 2003. Although the law was subsequently amended, at the relevant time the executing Court had no such authority. Moreover, earlier the executing Court had fixed the cases for taking steps under section 33 (4) of the Act, 2003 but without exhausting the process it suomotu jumped on the next phase and thereby committed gross illegally. For all the reasons all subsequent proceedings in the execution cases are liable to be declared to have been continued without lawful authority.

Mr. Masud Ahmed Sayeed, learned Advocate for the respondent-bank referring to order dated 24.01.2004 passed in Artha Jari Case No.114 of 2004 and order 28.04.2004 passed in Artha Jari Case No.165 of 2004 submits that two warrants of arrest to put the writ petitioner in civil imprisonment are still pending against him for execution. So, being a fugitive from law, the writ petitioner without surrendering before the executing Court has directly approached the High Court Division with the instant writ petitions, which are not maintainable. He then submits that the Artha Rin Jari Cases are civil cases too, so there is no wrong if a Joint District Judge deals with the Artha Jari Cases. Moreover, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a special law enacted for speedy recovery of loan. In the present case, the petitioner admits his loan liability to the respondent-bank and as such it makes no difference whether the execution cases are being dealt with by the Joint District Judge not vested with the power of Artha Rin Adalat.

We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates and gone through the records. Section 4 (7) of the Act, 2003 confers authority on the District Judge to assign any Joint District Judge to perform as a Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat in particular situations. In the present cases, the District Judge, Barisal had transferred the execution cases to the Joint District Judge, First Court, Barisal which reflects in order dated 19.05.2004 of Artha Jari Case No.114 of 2004 and in order dated 09.05.2004 of Artha Jari Case No.165 of 2004. The submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the Joint District Judge had no jurisdiction to proceed with the execution cases is, therefore, not tenable.

It appears from order dated 28.09.1998 passed in Artha Jari Case No.165 of 2004 that a notice of attachment was issued against the mortgaged property and thereafter, in order dated 25.01.1999 the executing Court observed that the notice was served. Thereafter, as many as eight attempts were taken for selling the mortgaged property in auction on publishing notices in news papers. The last attempt was taken on 10.04.2003 fixing the date for auction on 10.05.2003, on which date no bidder was available.

After coming into force of the Act, 2003 the executing Court by order dated 17.07.2003 fixed the next date for taking step under section 33 (4) of the Act, 2003 but the decree holder-bank consecutively did not take any step on next five dates. Ultimately the bank filed an application for issuance of a certificate under section 33 (5), which was allowed by order dated 02.02.2005 and the certificate was signed and stamped on 30.03.2005. Thereafter, the decree holder–bank filed another application for issuance of certificate under section 33 (7), which was allowed by order dated 12.03.2006.

In similar way a certificate under section 33 (7) of the Act, 2003 was issued on 12.03.2006 in Artha Jari Case No.114 of 2004. After more than six years from assumption of jurisdiction by the Joint District Judge, Barisal and more than four and half years from issuance of the certificates under section 33 (7) of the Act, 2003, the petitioner moved in this Court with these applications under article 102 of the Constitution. Nowhere within the four corners of the applications, it has been stated as to when the petitioner came to know about the proceedings in the execution cases, or that what prevented him from contesting the suit or from preferring an appeal against the decree under section 41 of the Act, 2003 or from filling an application under section 19 (2). It has also not been stated as to why the petitioner did not challenge the order of the District Judge, on the strength of which the Joint District Judge assumed jurisdiction over the matters. The delay of more than six years from the assumption of jurisdiction by the Joint District Judge has also not been explained. In such a position we are constrained to say that the judgment debtor-petitioner brought these writ petitions to frustrate the decree and to cause further delay of disposal of the execution cases, which in the meantime already expired more than fourteen years from its initiation in 1998. In this regard it is pointed out that the guarantor Abdul Mannan Khan was made defendant 2 in both the suits, whereas the writ petitioner did not make him a party in the instant writ petitions, which may open a scope on his (Abdul Mannan Khan’s) part to come again before the High Court Division taking the plea of unawareness of the decree. These are, therefore, not the fit cases to reply the alternative argument advanced by Mr. Khaled. We are not inclined to interfere with the impugned proceedings.

Before parting, we also note that the conduct of the officials and concerned lawyer of respondent-bank in conducting the execution cases is questionable. It is not clear as to why the bank failed to take step under section 33 (4) of the Act on several dates. It further appears that after issuing certificate under section 33 (7) of the Act, the executing Court did not send it for registration which is a requirement of law under the same section. In reply to a query made by the Court Mr. Sayeed appearing for the respondent-bank apprises us that no registration has yet been done after issuance of the certificates under section 33 (7) of the Act. Under the circumstances the respondent–bank is directed to hold enquiry as to why it failed to take any step under section 33 (4) of the Ain, when the matter was so fixed; why no step towards registration of the certificate under section 33 (7) of the Act was taken; why no steps for delivery of possession of the mortgaged property under section 33 (7Ka) (7Kha) of the Act was taken.

The executing Court is directed to send the certificates issued under section 33 (7) of the Act, 2003 for registration and proceed with the execution cases towards delivery of possession of the mortgaged property under section 33 (7Ka) after due compliance with the provision of section 33 (7Kha) of the Act, 2003.

With the above directions both the Rules are discharged.

Mohammad Bazlur Rahman, J.
I agree.
End.
